6. **Approximation is increasingly used to make media, graph, trajectory, and streaming analytics feasible at scale.** Approximate aggregation, approximate joins, approximate graph analytics, trajectory compression, and confidence-bounded video-stream query answering replace exact processing where speed and scale are critical (Reports 3, 39, 40, 41). **Importance: 92**

7. **Machine learning is moving from an auxiliary database technique to the core method for indexing, querying, and data management.** Learned indexes replace or complement B-trees and bitmap indexes; reinforcement learning selects materialized views and query plans; and integrated columnar/AI architectures connect extraction, featurization, and analysis in iterative feedback loops (Reports 7, 13, 35). **Importance: 87**

8. **Research increasingly treats dynamic social, behavioral, and sensor data as primary analytical objects.** Examples include evolving graphs, social-media streams, live-video chat, vessel AIS trajectories, user behavior, and dynamic diffusion, with systems designed for prediction, anomaly detection, monitoring, or real-time analysis rather than only static relational querying (Reports 20, 22, 25, 34, 50, 70, 73). **Importance: 90**

d90f5d5445b22b299e512ca01bcdbd9dced2f004.text:
- **Social media and social-network analysis — 100/100.** This is by far the most recurrent domain, appearing in reports covering Twitter, Facebook, Reddit, Gab, Weibo, Telegram, Instagram, and other platforms. Applications include social dynamics, sentiment, influence, diffusion, political communication, misinformation, profiling, and user behavior (Reports 1–2, 5–30, 33, 45, 47–48, 55–57, 60, 70).

- **Web search, information retrieval, and online content discovery — 82/100.** Recurring applications include microblog and temporal search, sponsored search, web crawling, query recommendation, document retrieval, media retrieval, content-quality evaluation, and search-based surveillance (Reports 18, 20, 22, 25–26, 38, 52, 59, 68, 70–71, 74).

- **Data management, databases, storage, and data integration — 80/100.** The reports repeatedly address key-value stores, spatial and XML indexes, storage managers, approximate querying, graph and property-graph data, visual-data management, streaming mining, data fusion, and web-data integration (Reports 3, 32, 34–35, 37, 48, 62–65, 67, 69–70, 73, 75).

- **Security, privacy, trust, and adversarial behavior — 77/100.** Applications include privacy-preserving data release and linkage, Sybil and sockpuppet detection, botnets, catfishing, malicious links, phishing, malware, misinformation, identity verification, trust management, and Byzantine resilience (Reports 7–8, 14, 16, 19–21, 30, 40, 54–55, 63).

- **Recommendation, personalization, and ranking — 72/100.** Recommendation occurs in venue and collaborative ranking, smart replies, social and group recommendation, tag and herb recommendation, television recommendation, sponsored search, food recommendation, and personalized media retrieval (Reports 1, 4, 17, 25, 33, 38, 41, 46–47, 69–70, 74).

- **News, public discourse, political communication, and information diffusion — 70/100.** Recurrent applications include news organization, event and crisis detection, election analysis, propaganda, rumor and disinformation tracking, political campaigning, and diffusion prediction, often using social-media data (Reports 6, 9–13, 15–20, 36, 45, 50, 57, 60).

- **Scholarly communication, research evaluation, and scientific knowledge — 55/100.** Reports cover software citation, scholarly infrastructure, research recommendation, citation impact, university rankings, academic peer review, scientific knowledge graphs, nanopublications, and citation-network visualization (Reports 20, 31, 44, 47, 54, 58, 66, 69).

- **Health, medicine, and wellbeing — 43/100.** This domain recurs through epidemic modeling, suicide-risk and mental-health analysis, antimicrobial-consumption surveillance, medical image processing, traditional Chinese medicine, health misinformation, and financial or personal wellbeing applications (Reports 1, 6, 9, 19, 21, 41, 48, 63, 65, 71).

bcccc2507433a29c0fe5b1dfa85381304bfa83b1.text:
Privacy, anonymization, fairness, accountability, and responsible data use are important but unevenly distributed across the corpus. They are generally secondary in work focused on scalability, indexing, storage, prediction, retrieval, or algorithmic performance, but become central when systems affect people’s privacy, reputation, safety, access, visibility, or opportunities.

**Privacy** is most explicit when data are personal, sensitive, behavioral, relational, geospatial, transactional, or health-related. Examples include browsing and search logs, locations, social networks, mobile-phone records, clinical data, financial information, sexual-relationship networks, and personal communications. Privacy becomes especially visible when data can support profiling, targeted advertising, friend or location inference, surveillance, or linkage across organizations and platforms. It is also prominent in federated learning, privacy-preserving querying, differential privacy, and controlled data release.

**Anonymization** is treated as a useful but imperfect protection. De-identified or anonymized data may preserve analytical utility, yet network structure, auxiliary datasets, background knowledge, repeated releases, or behavioral traces can enable re-identification and inference of identities, relationships, or sensitive attributes. Thus, anonymization creates both technical safeguards and governance complications, particularly when data are published, shared, or combined.

**Fairness** is most visible when algorithms rank, recommend, summarize, identify, advertise, allocate resources, or determine representation. The corpus addresses presentation and position bias, group disparities, racial and gender bias, unequal provider or user exposure, minority-class performance, political and school districting, forensic identification, peer review, and marketplace outcomes. Fairness is therefore understood not only as model accuracy, but also as inclusion, equal opportunity, balanced visibility, and resistance to institutional or sampling bias.

**Accountability** appears through audit trails, provenance, explanations, validation, tamper evidence, reproducibility, human oversight, and verifiable execution. These mechanisms become important when decisions must be traced, justified, independently checked, or protected against manipulation.

**Responsible data use** links these concerns to governance, consent, data quality, uncertainty, provenance, reproducibility, and controlled access. It becomes most visible in high-stakes or socially consequential settings—healthcare, clinical trials, credit, employment, elections, misinformation, advertising, political influence, public policy, fraud, and safety—and when data cross trust boundaries, are reused or combined, or operate under adversarial conditions.

0f4f2e48130fa818d30419610c3e223d7f66722e.text:
- **The reports do not provide a direct historical time series showing that foundational or application-driven research dominates in particular periods.** They are better read as evidence of an ongoing interaction between the two. **Importance: 100**

- **Foundational research remains a persistent base over time**, including new algorithms, theoretical models, optimization methods, embeddings, graph methods, privacy mechanisms, and probabilistic frameworks—for example, graphons, spectral methods, learned indexes, hashing, and diffusion models (Reports 7, 14, 18, 24, 61). **Importance: 90**

- **Application-driven research is widespread and increasingly tied to concrete operational settings**, such as healthcare matchmaking and collaboration, maritime intelligence, astronomy, vaccination uptake, financial processes, e-commerce search, and public-health communication (Reports 9, 34, 36, 44, 45, 59, 68). **Importance: 90**

- **A recurring progression is from offline or historical analysis toward real-time, streaming, adaptive, and dynamic applications.** Examples include time-oriented astronomical services supporting both historical and streaming analysis, dynamic graph updates, real-time video analytics, near-real-time vandalism detection, and adaptive vaccination estimation (Reports 22, 36, 45, 65, 73). **Importance: 88**

- **Application demands increasingly reshape foundational research priorities.** Practical requirements lead to work on scalability, latency, low memory, distributed execution, resource awareness, robustness, uncertainty, and privacy—for example, adaptive query optimization, GPU graph processing, approximate analytics, and auditable data systems (Reports 35, 39–41, 47, 48, 57). **Importance: 87**

- **Research often advances through iterative extensions of foundational methods for evolving application conditions.** Examples include static-to-dynamic community detection, ordinary-to-cross-chain blockchain systems, basic-to-asymmetric link prediction, and conventional-to-counterfactual or fair ranking (Reports 2, 19, 29, 46, 67, 73, 75). **Importance: 84**

- **Evaluation and deployment connect the two sides:** foundational methods are repeatedly tested on real datasets, competitions, or institutional systems, while application performance feeds back into method refinement. This is evident in biomedical retrieval, historical-document recognition, cloud-camera queries, genomic auditing, and database optimization (Reports 3, 7, 35, 47, 58, 65). **Importance: 82**

- **The balance appears complementary rather than a simple replacement of foundational research by applications:** foundational methods continue to generate general-purpose techniques, while applications increasingly determine which properties—fairness, privacy, efficiency, interpretability, and adaptability—matter most in later-stage research (Reports 17–19, 25, 27, 35, 54, 61). **Importance: 85**

bfc3873ebb5d8a5f77328791affb12173a981c02.text:
- **Unsupervised learning is explicitly represented through functional clustering.** Aggregated mobile-network data are clustered to classify neighborhoods and infer land-use patterns, showing ML used for exploratory structure discovery rather than only prediction. **Importance: 90/100**

- **Online and adaptive learning appears in ranking and platform problems.** Click data, interleaving, dueling/multi-dueling bandits, contextual methods, and risk-aware R-UCB support continual evaluation and optimization of ranked outputs. **Importance: 85/100**

- **Supervised learning is not clearly documented in the report.** The report describes inference tasks—such as disease-risk-zone detection and land-use inference—but does not specify labeled training or supervised models, so supervised use cannot be firmly established. **Importance: 75/100**

- **Weakly supervised learning is not explicitly reported.** Although mobile, platform, and behavioral traces may function as indirect signals, the report does not identify weak labels, noisy supervision, or related training procedures. **Importance: 65/100**

- **Representation learning is also not explicitly reported.** The work relies on engineered or domain-specific representations, such as urban sound dictionaries, smell tags, VAD-based viral facets, centrality, and graphlets, rather than describing learned embeddings or neural feature representations. **Importance: 80/100**

- **Overall, the documented progression is toward scalable, context-aware, and adaptive data analysis.** The corpus moves from engineered urban/behavioral features and clustering toward online ranking, fairness optimization, and bandit-based decision methods; however, the report provides little evidence of a transition to deep or learned representations. **Importance: 88/100**

c6397026361ee4ec8e6ca8e48f9813bd4278bffe.text:

- **Parkinson’s disease detection from mouse tracking** — Early-stage diagnosis using mouse-tracking data, expert-engineered features, and unsupervised representation learning appears as a distinct biomedical application niche. **Importance: 82/100** (Report 47)

70cf48a11b0539ea279f75d4454d1f8868f2086d.text:
1. **Recommendation, personalization, and ranking systems — 100/100**  
   The largest cluster covers collaborative filtering, factorization, neural and sequential recommendation, session modeling, cold start, multi-objective and fair recommendation, advertising, explainability, and reciprocal or social recommendation (Reports 7, 10–22, 39, 42, 46, 67, 68, 72).

2. **Query processing, databases, and data-management infrastructure — 96/100**  
   This cluster includes relational and conjunctive-query evaluation, query optimization, provenance, probabilistic databases, RDF/SPARQL, graph and path queries, temporal databases, LSM storage, distributed execution, sampling, data cleaning, and knowledge-base/table augmentation (Reports 1–4, 23, 27, 32, 51–57, 73, 75).

3. **Information retrieval, search, semantics, and entity matching — 93/100**  
   Related work addresses learning-to-rank, search sessions, retrieval fusion, multilingual and neural retrieval, entity profiling and resolution, scientific concept extraction, semantic tagging, question answering, and entity-set or trendline search (Reports 31, 34, 40, 45–48, 50, 61, 67, 71, 74, 75).

4. **Network science, diffusion, temporal graphs, and intervention — 92/100**  
   This cluster spans PageRank and influence, social and citation networks, community emergence, relational events, signed-network dynamics, reliability, opinion formation, epidemic cascades, network dismantling, mobility, and dynamic transportation networks (Reports 8, 24, 26, 28–30, 37, 49, 54, 56, 64, 65, 68, 69).

5. **Scholarly communication, scientometrics, and research evaluation — 89/100**  
   Work here studies citation and impact indicators, rankings, research diversity, funding, peer-review competence and bias, researcher mobility, open science, topic mapping, dissertation impact, and scientific collaboration (Reports 30, 35–39, 43, 58–63).

6. **Applied prediction, media, health, and decision-support analytics — 78/100**  
   A more application-oriented cluster uses machine learning and data mining for news summarization and bias, ESG and adverse-media risk, health and disease prediction, crisis response, building inspection, advertising, protest prediction, and business intelligence (Reports 5, 33, 40–44, 47, 64, 70).

7. **Ranking, graphs, embeddings, and evaluation form the strongest cross-cluster bridge — 98/100**  
   Ranking connects recommendation, search, PageRank, scholarly impact, entity retrieval, and query optimization. Graph representations and embeddings connect recommender user–item graphs, web and citation networks, entity resolution, knowledge graphs, diffusion models, and dynamic-network prediction (Reports 7, 8, 13, 25, 34, 46, 58, 65, 67, 68).

8. **Shared data-system foundations bridge otherwise separate applications — 94/100**  
   Sampling, distributed processing, temporal modeling, provenance, probabilistic representations, indexing, and scalable query engines recur across databases, graph analytics, retrieval, recommendation, scientific analysis, and real-time applications. Evaluation practices—offline/online testing, robustness, ranking metrics, causal intervention, and benchmark datasets—provide an additional methodological bridge (Reports 1–4, 6, 21–23, 32, 51–57, 66, 72).

bb6d57f005f21ff9f23b424f3fb1064f6b6f5c78.text:
## Relative prominence of systems-oriented research

Systems-oriented contributions are **highly prominent and recurring, but not dominant across the corpus**. Many reports present implemented platforms, databases, execution engines, storage systems, APIs, distributed infrastructures, stream processors, graph engines, and production services. Examples include Blocklite, SystemDS, ResilientDB, ChainifyDB, Apache Calcite, GraphLab/PowerGraph, ModelarDB, VDMS, and various recommendation, retrieval, and query-processing systems.

However, systems research is generally **less pervasive than algorithmic and empirical research**:

1. **Algorithmic research is the broadest category.** Most reports introduce or improve algorithms, models, optimization procedures, embeddings, ranking methods, graph techniques, prediction methods, or learning systems. This pattern occurs across recommendation, retrieval, graph mining, influence maximization, data cleaning, and network analysis.

2. **Empirical evaluation is nearly universal and often central.** Algorithms and systems are repeatedly assessed using real datasets, benchmarks, simulations, online experiments, deployments, and operational workloads. Measures include accuracy, speed, scalability, latency, ranking quality, resource use, and business or user outcomes. Empirical work is therefore at least as widespread as systems research.

3. **Systems contributions frequently combine implementation with algorithmic novelty.** Many systems serve as vehicles for deploying or evaluating algorithms—for example approximate analytics, graph-query frameworks, recommender pipelines, query optimizers, adaptive indexes, and production ranking systems. Thus, systems work is often not standalone infrastructure research, but an algorithm–system–evaluation combination.

4. **Theoretical work is substantial but more specialized.** It includes complexity and hardness results, approximation guarantees, convergence and spectral analysis, formal privacy or consistency models, and equilibrium analysis. It is usually attached to algorithmic contributions rather than being the dominant contribution type.

5. **User-centered research is visible but generally narrower.** It appears in personalization, recommendation, interactive visualization, human-in-the-loop systems, explainability, fairness, usability, and user studies. In some application areas it is highly visible, but overall it is less widespread than algorithmic, empirical, and systems-oriented work.

Overall, the corpus is best characterized as **algorithmically led, empirically validated, and substantially systems-oriented**. Systems research forms a strong secondary pillar, especially in databases, data management, distributed computing, streaming, storage, and production infrastructure, but it does not outweigh the broader algorithmic and empirical emphasis.

3f220f6cc653f08c545e9e8cd698368d5aed749d.text:
## Distribution across the four areas

- **Social and information networks are the dominant area** (generally **92–100/100**). They recur across social-media analysis, graph learning, communities, diffusion, influence, recommendation, opinion dynamics, mobility, misinformation, temporal networks, and network analytics. This is the corpus’s broadest and most pervasive theme.

- **Information retrieval is a major, technically diverse strand** (about **78–95/100**). It covers ranking, query processing, semantic and neural retrieval, question answering, personalization, recommendation, multimedia and visual search, biomedical and scholarly retrieval, and specialized search applications.

- **Databases and data-management systems form another substantial concentration** (about **82–95/100**). Work includes query processing and optimization, indexing, storage, graph databases, distributed and stream processing, provenance, data integration, RDF/SPARQL, approximate analytics, and structured-data search.

- **Digital libraries and scholarly information are the smallest or most concentrated area** (about **68–90/100**). They focus on scholarly search, repositories, citation and co-authorship networks, bibliometrics, research assessment, open-access resources, archival collections, metadata, knowledge organization, and research-data infrastructure.

## Strongest overlaps

The material identifies two repeatedly dominant intersections:

1. **Social/information networks and information retrieval** (roughly **86–98/100**). Social platforms and network data provide searchable content and behavioral signals, while retrieval supports social-media search, recommendation, personalized and influence-aware ranking, news and misinformation tracking, event detection, and information verification.

2. **Databases and social/information networks** (roughly **84–98/100**). Their overlap is centred on graph databases, graph querying and embeddings, temporal and distributed graph processing, stream systems, scalable network analytics, provenance, and social-data management.

Other important connections are:

- **Information retrieval and databases** (about **82–94/100**): indexing, query optimization, structured and semi-structured search, semantic parsing, entity integration, and data-aware ranking.
- **Information retrieval and digital libraries** (about **86–98/100**): scholarly discovery, citation-based retrieval, publication recommendation, bibliographic metadata, scientific search, and knowledge-graph question answering.
- **Databases and digital libraries** (about **76–87/100**): repositories, metadata, provenance, archival storage, RDF/ontologies, citation databases, and scalable scholarly-data infrastructure.

Overall, the corpus is network-dominated, with retrieval and databases providing broad technical and application-oriented bridges, while digital-library work is narrower but strongly connected to scholarly retrieval and infrastructure.

18da9139e4cc8218fd94c763f6e6fc0f995ed0a2.text:
The corpus relies **substantially, though not exclusively, on widely used benchmark datasets and platforms**. Recurrent benchmarks include TREC and ClueWeb collections, MovieLens, Netflix, Amazon, Yelp, UCI, Reuters-21578, CoNLL, BioASQ, QALD, MS MARCO, OHSUMED, Wikipedia-linked resources, MS COCO, and multimedia or recommendation datasets such as YouTube-8M, Recipe1M and Last.fm. Recommendation, information retrieval, question answering, classification, graph learning and multimedia research therefore often use a relatively small set of familiar evaluation resources. Shared tracks, challenge datasets and standardized relevance judgments improve comparability across studies.

There is also considerable **platform concentration**. Twitter/X is especially prominent, alongside Facebook, Reddit, YouTube, Google services, Amazon, Alibaba, Spotify, LinkedIn, Stack Exchange, Airbnb, Uber and mobile-network systems. Common software and infrastructure—including Spark, Hadoop, Lucene, Neo4j, Jupyter, TensorFlow, PyTorch, Docker, AWS and major platform APIs—further reinforce dependence on particular technical ecosystems.

However, the corpus is not wholly benchmark-driven. It includes substantial domain-specific, geographic and locally collected data: clinical and hospital records, mobility and telecommunications data, enterprise logs, legal and financial documents, disaster and election corpora, astronomy and ecological data, invoices, scientific datasets, and synthetic or semi-synthetic networks. This diversity reduces, but does not remove, concentration.

The main risk is **narrow generalization**. Repeated testing on datasets such as TREC, MovieLens, Amazon, Wikipedia, Stack Exchange or Twitter may make improvements appear broadly applicable while actually reflecting particular user populations, interaction structures, labels, sampling practices and domain distributions. Platform-based studies may similarly inherit platform-specific interfaces, ranking conventions, APIs and behaviours, limiting transfer to other countries, populations, platforms or application settings. Event- and region-specific datasets create additional limits.

Reproducibility is consequently uneven. Open, named benchmarks and public datasets provide relatively strong foundations for replication, but many studies depend on proprietary logs, commercial systems, health or enterprise data, changing web archives, live services, restricted APIs and online experiments. Access loss, deleted content, API restrictions, dataset drift and changing platform conditions can prevent exact reconstruction. Even public datasets do not guarantee reproducibility when versions, splits, annotation, preprocessing, weighting, configurations and evaluation protocols are unspecified. Weak code documentation, maintenance and runtime configuration add further problems.

Thus, the corpus combines useful standardization with significant risks of dataset concentration, platform dependence and incomplete independent verification.

9815550f8fc8350659e030a21c5889943e284b7d.text:
- **Graph and network analysis is the dominant problem family**: reports repeatedly address community detection and evolution, centrality, similarity, influence diffusion, robustness, anomaly detection, graph querying, dynamic updates, and network privacy/anonymization (Reports 5, 8, 14, 19, 20, 23, 26, 34, 37–39, 43, 59, 65, 75). **Importance: 100/100**

- **Recommendation and personalization are also highly prevalent**: recurring problems include user and item representation, social and influence-aware recommendation, long-tail coverage, sequential prediction, news and music recommendation, product retrieval, and personalized search/query suggestions (Reports 10, 12, 17, 20, 30, 48, 51, 54, 57, 58, 60, 65). **Importance: 96/100**

- **Search, retrieval, ranking, and information access form another major cluster**: the collection covers document and image retrieval, entity resolution, similarity search, dataset search, conversational search, query recommendation, top-*k* processing, and ranking of scholarly or knowledge-library entities (Reports 13, 16, 21, 25, 27, 29, 40, 50, 54, 60, 65, 73). **Importance: 92/100**

- **Scalable data management and query processing are common cross-cutting problems**: research addresses distributed ingestion, streaming and sliding-window summaries, uncertain and dynamic databases, schema coexistence and synchronization, graph/RDF querying, parallel query correctness, workload embeddings, and data-flow optimization (Reports 9, 11, 27, 28, 35, 49, 53, 60, 67). **Importance: 89/100**

- **Temporal, evolving, and real-time data analysis is a recurring concern**: examples include dynamic communities and graphs, changing user preferences, streaming anomaly detection, temporal profiles, dynamic SimRank, mobility and check-in data, and evolving interaction networks (Reports 8, 12, 14, 23, 29, 37, 48, 51, 57, 64, 71). **Importance: 86/100**

- **Social information integrity and harmful-behavior detection are frequently studied**: the reports cover spam, cyberbullying, abusive messages, rumors, opinion spam, shilling attacks, disinformation, credibility, political polarization, and community deception (Reports 5, 10–12, 14, 18, 22, 36, 43, 45, 46, 59). **Importance: 83/100**

- **Scholarly communication, evaluation, and knowledge diffusion are substantial but less numerous than graph, recommendation, or data-management work**: recurring problems include bibliometric impact measurement, open-access compliance, reviewer selection, citation and coauthor networks, publication patterns, peer review, scientific attention, and scholarly meme propagation (Reports 13, 40, 42, 47, 56, 61–63, 66). **Importance: 76/100**

- **Comparatively underexplored within the collection are specialized preservation, reproducibility, governance, and domain-infrastructure problems**: archival fixity and dissemination, autonomic digital preservation, computational reproducibility incentives, blockchain-based clinical-trial compliance, persistent-memory data structures, and evidence-based R&D project selection each appear in isolated reports, unlike the repeated graph, recommendation, search, and streaming themes (Reports 4, 6, 7, 15, 32, 53). **Importance: 94/100**

46b13ee5af243dd3c474c7c4650fbea187f9ef55.text:
- **Social-media and online-network analysis became the dominant umbrella theme, especially toward 2020 (importance: 100/100).** The collection moves from general social-network structure, ties, communities, and diffusion (Reports 1, 24, 25) toward extensive analysis of Twitter, Facebook, Reddit, Telegram, Instagram, and other platforms, including events, engagement, public discourse, and user behavior (Reports 9–21, 26–30, 45, 56–57).

- **Information diffusion, influence, and collective behavior remained central but became more temporally complex and application-driven (importance: 96/100).** Earlier work emphasizes independent-cascade, linear-threshold, epidemic, voter, and influence-maximization models (Reports 24–25). Later work adds multiple cascades, temporal influence, coordination, diffusion prediction, rumor blocking, and political-campaign optimization (Reports 6, 8, 16, 19, 24, 45).

- **Misinformation, propaganda, political manipulation, and bots grew substantially in prominence by the later period (importance: 98/100).** The reports describe troll accounts, Russian interference, junk news, disinformation, extremist propaganda, fake profiles, botnets, spam, coordinated campaigns, and election manipulation (Reports 10–20, 45, 55, 57). These topics are much more prominent in the later social-media-focused communities than in the foundational graph-analysis reports.

- **Network science and graph algorithms were persistent foundational themes, with a shift toward richer and more scalable models (importance: 91/100).** Early themes include community detection, structural balance, centrality, cohesive subgraphs, graph inference, and influence maximization (Reports 1, 22, 24–25, 30). Later work expands to signed and higher-order networks, heterogeneous alignment, temporal graphs, hypergraphs, motifs, graph neural networks, and scalable graph processing (Reports 1–2, 22, 43–45, 49, 60).

- **NLP, information retrieval, topic modeling, and recommendation increased in prominence as social content became central (importance: 88/100).** Earlier methods include sentiment analysis, topic models, classification, and event detection (Reports 10–12, 18, 21). Later work adds neural embeddings, knowledge-aware representations, multimodal text-image learning, transfer ranking, generative retrieval, and proactive dialogue recommendation (Reports 4, 9, 36, 38, 47, 52).

- **Privacy, trust, security, and platform integrity became more prominent alongside large-scale social-data collection (importance: 87/100).** The collection progresses from privacy-preserving release and social-graph protection to temporal privacy leakage, Sybil resistance, catfish and sockpuppet detection, adversarial methods, malicious links, bot detection, GDPR, and credibility assessment (Reports 7, 8, 14, 19–20, 30, 40, 55).

- **Data-management and systems research formed a substantial parallel theme, emphasizing scale and efficiency rather than social phenomena (importance: 82/100).** Across the period, the reports cover spatial and XML indexing, streaming mining, graph storage, web crawling, and query processing; later systems emphasize low-latency key-value stores, learned indexes, video ingestion, visual-data management, and high-throughput analytics (Reports 3, 32, 34–39, 64–65, 70, 73).

- **Domain-specific applications remained diverse but were relatively less prominent than social media, diffusion, and information integrity by 2020 (importance: 72/100).** Smaller strands address health, disasters, urban mobility, education, finance, transportation, scholarly communication, traditional medicine, and innovation systems (Reports 6, 9, 29, 41, 53, 58, 60–61, 71). Their methods increasingly reuse the collection’s dominant tools—networks, temporal analysis, prediction, recommendation, and text mining.

a51709e311fa65d6623b66fba670e68e2099d45a.text:
1. **Misinformation research has broadened from rumor detection to coordinated, adversarial, and platform-scale information integrity.** Work now includes rumor-source detection, rumor blocking, coordinated hashtag propaganda, spam, Wikidata vandalism, hybrid fact validation, and adversarial fake-user attacks against recommender systems. **(Importance: 96/100)** — Reports 2, 5, 22, 25, 37

2. **Misinformation is increasingly studied in relation to public health and real-world communication campaigns.** COVID-19 fake news, bioweapons conspiracies, Facebook advertising, and negative media attention linked to irregular vaccination uptake show a move toward evaluating information ecosystems and their societal consequences. **(Importance: 92/100)** — Reports 36, 59

3. **Research on polarization and collective opinion has become more formal, dynamic, and network-based.** Studies model polar opinion dynamics, changing social power and self-appraisals, partisan political structures, community formation, diffusion, and viral propagation rather than treating opinions as isolated user attributes. **(Importance: 88/100)** — Reports 24, 56, 61, 73, 75

4. **Scholarship increasingly models online behavior as temporal, contextual, and evolving.** Examples include unfollow prediction from spatial, temporal, content, and history signals; behavioral archetypes across sessions; information-release dynamics on WeChat; and short-term performance decline versus long-term learning in collaborative communities. **(Importance: 90/100)** — Reports 26, 50, 51, 69

5. **Marketing and recommendation research has shifted toward adaptive, personalized, and experimentally evaluated decision-making.** Bandits, counterfactual learning-to-rank, contextual recommendation, engagement prediction, conversion modeling, and promotion-response models are used to optimize placement, ranking, watch time, and user preferences under incomplete or biased feedback. **(Importance: 94/100)** — Reports 1, 9, 15, 17, 23, 35

6. **Marketing scholarship now pays more attention to manipulation, competing interests, fairness, and diversity.** Research considers multi-stakeholder recommendation, adversarial fake profiles, popularity and visibility bias, fair search and news feeds, diversity indicators, and the gap between user benefit and profitability. **(Importance: 93/100)** — Reports 17, 18, 19, 37

7. **Online safety has expanded from privacy protection to active social protection and trustworthy infrastructure.** The reports cover tracker removal, privacy-preserving publishing, protection against abusive contacts, anonymous-contribution risks, searchable encryption, secure computation, auditable logs, and detection of insider or malicious failures. **(Importance: 95/100)** — Reports 3, 17, 27, 48, 59, 61, 66

8. **Across these topics, platform scholarship increasingly combines machine learning with graphs, behavioral data, intervention, and reproducible measurement.** Network embeddings, community detection, dynamic graphs, human-in-the-loop systems, risk-aware answering, platform experiments, and explicit bias/error metrics support more operational analysis of platform behavior and governance. **(Importance: 91/100)** — Reports 4, 8, 18, 19, 22, 25, 35, 73

0a8199ab93f7647c5a6fc34bf7d380c32fc4dc91.text:
- **Social and interaction graphs/networks — 98/100.** The collection most often studies social, communication, collaboration, diffusion, and interaction networks, including dynamic and multiplex graphs. Examples include social-network datasets, email and smartphone interactions, coauthorship and citation graphs, online communities, darkweb forums, and user–item networks (Reports 5, 8, 19, 23, 26, 29, 34, 39, 40, 46, 55, 59, 61, 74).

- **Web, social-media, and online-community platforms — 94/100.** Twitter, Instagram, Vine, Weibo, Ask.fm, online forums, online political communities, search engines, and other user-generated-content platforms are frequent environments for studying misinformation, abuse, credibility, mobility, recommendation, and discourse (Reports 10–13, 25, 29, 34, 36, 45, 46, 51, 54, 65, 71).

- **Scholarly, bibliometric, and scientific-literature datasets — 90/100.** Repeatedly studied resources include citation and coauthorship networks, DBLP, arXiv, CiteSeerX, Microsoft Academic Search, INSPIRE-HEP, scholarly publishing records, patent literature, peer-review data, and scientometrics datasets (Reports 1, 13, 40, 42, 47, 52, 56, 61–63, 66).

- **Recommendation, e-commerce, and media-consumption data — 87/100.** Common datasets and platforms involve user–product interactions, shopping and fashion data, e-commerce reviews, music streaming and radio, news consumption, movies, books, and product recommendation systems. Examples include eBay, Alibaba, Xianyu, Douban, MovieTweetings, BookCrossing, and music-streaming logs (Reports 5, 10, 12, 16, 17, 20, 30, 51, 57, 58, 74).

- **Streaming, time-series, sensor, and operational-system data — 83/100.** The reports frequently use distributed streams, compressed time series, smart-meter consumption, Internet traffic, video streams, SQL workloads, and other continuously arriving data. Systems include Plato, Kafka-based ingestion, Spark Streaming, ECM sketches, autonomous cameras, and high-performance computing environments (Reports 3, 11, 14, 28, 44, 60, 67, 72).

- **Mobility, transportation, and location-based environments — 76/100.** Studied settings include POI check-ins, mobile-phone mobility, commuting, shopping-mall visitation, air traffic, traffic networks, and geospatially structured social networks. Key examples are Santiago de Chile mall mobility, Weibo check-ins, Chicago traffic networks, and POI recommendation datasets (Reports 22, 23, 48, 64, 71).

- **Biomedical, healthcare, and clinical datasets/platforms — 68/100.** The collection includes multi-site clinical-trial data, biomedical text and protein-interaction corpora, medical-science publication and altmetric data, biological sample metadata, and health-related network applications (Reports 7, 13, 68, 73).

- **Real-world infrastructure and deployed computing environments — 65/100.** Research is also evaluated on or applied to power grids, road networks, Internet and cyber-threat infrastructure, autonomous/off-grid cameras, PlanetLab, embedded hardware, persistent-memory systems, and open or distributed data platforms (Reports 14, 18, 22, 43, 53, 55, 67, 72, 75).

c7607d42d81a2eb36559a535873b0b5d1563f53b.text:
Across the corpus, machine learning evolves from conventional, feature-based prediction toward hybrid, representation-centred, and adaptive systems.

**Supervised learning remains the foundation.** Classical classifiers—including SVMs, Naive Bayes, logistic models, trees, random forests, and AdaBoost—support sentiment, spam, fraud, abuse, health, legal, and anomaly classification. Supervision also extends to citation and engagement prediction, relation and answer selection, search reranking, learning-to-rank, recommendation, and sequence labelling. Over time, it is applied to more specialized objectives, including fairness, counterfactual ranking, cold-start prediction, risk-aware answering, and temporal forecasting. Deep supervised models increasingly replace manually engineered features in language, vision, video, graphs, and recommendation.

**Unsupervised learning is used where labels are unavailable or costly.** It supports clustering, topic and community discovery, anomaly detection, similarity search, dimensionality reduction, entity consolidation, and latent-structure inference. The corpus includes topic models, matrix and tensor factorization, Gaussian mixtures, autoencoders, random-walk network embeddings, unsupervised retrieval, and fully unsupervised tasks such as toponym resolution and named-entity recognition. Thus, unsupervised methods increasingly discover reusable structure rather than merely serving as alternatives to classifiers.

**Weakly supervised and semi-supervised learning bridge the gap between these settings.** Labels are induced from pseudo-documents, seed words, heuristic rules, external knowledge, crowdsourcing, pattern nomination, and self-training. Graph-based methods propagate labels from a small annotated subset, while active learning reduces annotation errors and one-shot or few-shot methods operate with minimal examples. Implicit signals—clicks, views, interactions, engagement, fixation time, and user behaviour—also function as noisy or indirect supervision. Bandit and counterfactual methods extend this idea to biased, partial, and continually changing feedback.

**Representation learning becomes increasingly central.** Learned embeddings replace hand-crafted features for words, documents, queries, users, items, entities, tables, trajectories, images, audio, and multimodal data. Deep, self-supervised, and unsupervised approaches—including word and paragraph vectors, autoencoders, variational models, Transformers, and metric learning—produce representations for downstream retrieval, clustering, recommendation, and prediction. Graph representation learning becomes a major direction: node, edge, knowledge-graph, heterogeneous, temporal, and graph-neural embeddings capture relational structure for link prediction, fraud detection, recommendation, and anomaly detection.

Overall, the corpus shows convergence rather than replacement: modern pipelines learn representations, exploit supervised and imperfect signals, integrate heterogeneous modalities and graphs, and adapt through interaction, feedback, transfer, and online decision-making.

504c75500eb3ad07a08bdffbc4f94b69357dbdde.text:
1. **Social-media analytics combining network analysis, NLP, machine learning, and diffusion modeling** — Social graphs, text, sentiment, misinformation, bots, political behavior, and information cascades are repeatedly analyzed together. *(Reports 6–21, 45, 55–57)* — **Importance: 100**

2. **Social influence and information diffusion combining network science, temporal modeling, and optimization** — Influence maximization, cascade prediction, rumor blocking, contagion, election control, and coordinated behavior use graph models with probabilistic, temporal, and optimization methods. *(Reports 6, 8, 10, 12, 15–19, 24–25, 45)* — **Importance: 95**

3. **Information retrieval and search combined with social/network analysis and language modeling** — Research links microblog retrieval, temporal search, topic–actor networks, social collaborative retrieval, knowledge-aware retrieval, and personalized media search. *(Reports 18, 20, 25, 38, 47, 66, 70, 74)* — **Importance: 88**

4. **Graph machine learning combining heterogeneous, temporal, or higher-order network analysis** — Graph attention, graph convolution, neural network alignment, temporal graph prediction, hypergraphs, embeddings, and multi-graph models are applied to social, medical, and other relational data. *(Reports 2, 22, 41, 43, 47, 60)* — **Importance: 86**

5. **Database and data-management systems combined with machine learning or statistical modeling** — Examples include learned indexes, database debiasing with Bayesian networks, ML-based feature selection, query learning, and database systems supporting ML pipelines. *(Reports 32, 34, 48, 65, 73)* — **Importance: 78**

6. **Recommendation, ranking, and personalization combining retrieval, user modeling, and machine learning** — Tag, social, television, herb, sponsored-search, popularity, and media recommendations integrate ranking, embeddings, context, user behavior, and online learning. *(Reports 4, 17, 26–27, 33, 38, 41, 46, 74)* — **Importance: 76**

7. **Multimodal and visual analytics combining computer vision, text processing, graphs, and retrieval** — Image–text similarity, visual data management, video querying, visual graph summarization, and image/social-media analysis connect visual representations with language, metadata, storage, or network structure. *(Reports 9, 26, 46, 64–66, 74)* — **Importance: 70**

8. **Privacy, security, and trust combined with network analysis and machine learning** — Sybil and sockpuppet detection, privacy-preserving linkage, adversarial networks, bot detection, trust graphs, and secure data release combine graph structure with classification, inference, or cryptographic/privacy methods. *(Reports 7, 14, 19–20, 30, 40, 55, 63)* — **Importance: 68**

117884dd3c487efa96c9ef515f8dd9c6b1c6478d.text:
Research on graphs and networks developed from analysing relatively static structure toward building scalable, adaptive and application-oriented network intelligence.

**Community detection** initially focused on global structural partitioning using modularity, spectral methods, hierarchical clustering, stochastic block models, cliques and label propagation. It later expanded to overlapping, hierarchical, local and seeded communities, as well as attributed, signed, multilayer, higher-order and fuzzy structures. Dynamic methods began tracking community emergence, evolution and anomalies across time, while newer approaches incorporated content, diffusion, spatial proximity, core–periphery structure, causal information, fairness and privacy.

**Influence research** moved beyond static rankings based on degree, PageRank, HITS, betweenness, k-shell and related centralities. Researchers developed context-, topic-, time- and multilayer-aware measures, and studied influence as a strategic process involving competing agents, opinion dynamics, network dismantling, immunization and referral incentives. Influence maximization became adaptive and intervention-oriented, using observed cascades, budget constraints, diversified seeds, fairness objectives, approximation methods and large-scale computation.

**Diffusion research** likewise progressed from basic contagion and threshold models to temporal, probabilistic and controllable processes. SIR/SIS, Hawkes processes, branching processes, percolation and temporal point processes were used to model epidemics, rumors, misinformation, malware, adoption and cross-platform news. Research increasingly addressed source localization, cascade prediction, infection-probability estimation, rumor blocking, epidemic control, competing cascades, complex contagion and the effects of topology, dormancy, awareness and content.

**Embeddings** evolved from random-walk, spectral and proximity representations into attributed, heterogeneous, signed, temporal, multiplex, hyperbolic, multimodal and knowledge-graph representations. Graph autoencoders, graph neural networks, recurrent models and higher-order embeddings captured motifs, hyperedges, relations, behavior and global context. These representations supported link prediction, classification, recommendation, fraud detection, retrieval, entity alignment and mobility analysis, while quantization, hashing, sparse projection and distributed systems improved memory use and industrial-scale performance.

**Privacy** broadened from anonymization, privacy-aware publishing and differential privacy to protection of nodes, edges, communities, queries, locations, identities and event streams. Research examined de-anonymization, linkage and attribute-inference attacks, repeated-release risks, secure computation, federated systems, encrypted search, blockchain audit trails and privacy-preserving recommendations. Across all areas, scalability, streaming, distributed computation and higher-order modelling became central responses to increasingly large, dynamic and heterogeneous networks.

1c0d6a3fe030cda2013abdc38cad95a7e532e1e5.text:
1. **Research increasingly targets unstructured text and language rather than only relational records.** Examples include neural information retrieval and reranking, BERT-based passage retrieval, document embeddings, named-entity recognition, sentiment and spam detection, literary corpora, legal documents, and weakly supervised text classification (Reports 3, 24, 25, 38, 47, 51, 74). **Importance: 95**

2. **Multimodal problems are a prominent research direction.** Work combines text, images, video, audio, tables, and user behavior, including cross-modal hashing, image–text retrieval, query-based video-moment retrieval, multimodal event detection on Twitter, multimodal recommendation, and music analysis using timbral, harmonic, and rhythmic signals (Reports 5, 16, 30, 32, 52, 65–67). **Importance: 94**

3. **Streaming, temporal, and real-time data have become central targets.** The reports describe real-time behavior-change detection, distributed stream processing, exactly-once delivery, temporal point processes, continuous-time link streams, evolving networks, streaming data cleaning, and online model retraining over changing data streams (Reports 1, 7, 19, 21, 35, 42, 55, 75). **Importance: 93**

4. **The data sources increasingly consist of digital traces and dynamic user activity rather than static structured datasets.** Research uses Twitter streams, search and click logs, web traffic, Q&A activity, mobile sensing, transaction histories, social-media posts, app reviews, and online communities to model behavior, diffusion, recommendation, and security (Reports 1, 7, 13, 22, 26, 40, 47, 54). **Importance: 90**

5. **Representation learning is replacing or augmenting traditional schema- and feature-engineering approaches.** Neural language models, graph embeddings, contextualized encoders, attention, transformers, memory networks, and learned hash codes are used to represent text, tables, graphs, products, videos, and user histories (Reports 1, 5, 16, 22, 24, 30, 38, 39). **Importance: 89**

6. **Traditional database and query-processing techniques are being extended to complex, raw, or heterogeneous data.** Examples include OLA-RAW, which enables immediate SQL queries over unreorganized raw files; DeepLens for visual data management; query interfaces over heterogeneous graphs and scientific tables; natural-language interfaces for relational data; and query labeling based on learned SQL embeddings (Reports 27, 29, 31, 49, 53). **Importance: 86**

7. **Structured-data research remains present but is increasingly combined with learned, unstructured, or dynamic components.** Classical query optimization, OLTP/OLAP, factorized databases, XML-OLAP, Datalog, indexes, and transaction systems continue (Reports 3, 10, 12, 28, 33, 35, 46, 58), while learned optimizers, neural table understanding, provenance embeddings, and hybrid data-science systems connect them to newer data modalities (Reports 19, 28, 33, 38, 49). **Importance: 84**

8. **Applications increasingly require online adaptation, interaction, and human-facing interpretation.** Systems perform adaptive recommendation, interactive search, human-in-the-loop ranking, visual graph exploration, explainable anomaly detection, causal analysis of online behavior, and continuously updated profiles or models (Reports 7, 13, 21, 23, 27, 31, 55). **Importance: 82**

65b2cbbbc691e18a11d335c86c44b639ef04097d.text:
- **Approximately 20 of 75 reports—about 27%—focus substantially on recommendation, ranking, personalization, or user modeling.** This includes reports centered on these topics as well as reports where they form a major cluster, such as 1, 6, 9, 11, 15, 17–19, 25–30, 37, 49–50, 62, 67, and 72. **Importance: 100**

- **The collection begins with classical and bandit-based recommendation and ranking**, including learning from logged or biased feedback, inverse-propensity correction, interleaved testing, UCB methods, PageRank, similarity-based recommendation, and query completion. **Importance: 90**

- **Recommendation and ranking evolve toward counterfactual and debiased learning.** Reports address presentation bias, propensity-weighted metrics, off-policy evaluation, examination bias, historical-feedback bias, and ambiguity in relevance labels. **Importance: 94**

- **Deep representation learning becomes central.** Neural ranking, autoencoders, embeddings, graph-based representations, and multimodal models are used for user preferences, traveler profiles, item similarity, relation modeling, and product or story recommendation. **Importance: 91**

- **Personalization becomes more contextual and sequential.** Systems use short- and long-term history, implicit signals, purchase or consultation histories, play duration, session behavior, temporal context, and user–entity affinities rather than relying only on static ratings. **Importance: 93**

- **User modeling expands beyond preference prediction to behavior and evolution.** The reports model unfollow behavior, influencer interests, avatar choices, behavioral archetypes, trust, and changing user or community states, including both spatial and temporal signals. **Importance: 88**

- **Evaluation increasingly includes fairness, diversity, robustness, and multiple stakeholders.** The collection covers fair ranked search, fair News Feeds, popularity and visibility bias, diversity and balance measures, multi-stakeholder utility, adversarial fake-user attacks, and protection-oriented recommendations. **Importance: 95**

- **Overall, the field shifts from optimizing immediate accuracy or utility toward richer, efficient, and socially aware systems**—combining deep and multimodal models with contextual personalization, counterfactual evaluation, long-term effects, fairness, diversity, robustness, and low-latency deployment. **Importance: 97**

7ed0ea57de7744e4f2b7a9fd0f5815ba0935c04b.text:
1. **Computational stigmergy for spatiotemporal mobility-hotspot detection** — Uses digital pheromone deposits on credit-card transaction locations to identify permanent and intermittent hotspots; this appears as a highly self-contained method/application area. **Importance: 96**

2. **Core Influence and leaf-removal decomposition for minimal vertex cover** — Focuses on Leaf-Removal cores, core breaking, maximal matching, and the P/NP distinction, with little connection to the corpus’s dominant recommendation, retrieval, or social-media themes. **Importance: 94**

3. **Counting query answers under null-valued databases** — The specialized distinction between counting completions and counting valuations, Codd tables, #P-related complexity, and FPRAS approximability is unusually isolated. **Importance: 93**

4. **CyberChair and pattern-based conference-paper reviewing** — A narrowly focused groupware system for review administration, conflict resolution, paper selection, and review-process patterns. **Importance: 91**

5. **Cross-national measurement of crowdworker motivation** — The MCMS, Self-Determination Theory, measurement invariance, and comparisons across countries and income groups form a distinct human-labor measurement niche. **Importance: 89**

6. **Connected vehicles, V2V communication, shared mobility, and traffic-dependent communication conditions** — Combines transportation infrastructure with communication modeling and clustered epidemic differential equations, making it a specialized application cluster. **Importance: 87**

7. **Creative-art appreciation prediction and selfie-based sleep-condition assessment** — The Behance artwork-appreciation study and facial-cue-based sleep-deprivation prediction are two highly specific applications with minimal overlap with surrounding communities. **Importance: 86**

8. **Hardware-aware automated data-structure design** — Design primitives, learned cost models, hardware profiles, random access, and automated data-layout synthesis constitute a distinctive systems-design area. **Importance: 82**

e2dd7593890172beee2ffa671f6e362b6fe9b0f7.text:
1. **The reports do not provide a dated chronology, so they cannot establish a precise historical shift in the balance over time.** They instead show foundational and application-driven work coexisting across different research stages and communities. **Importance: 96**

2. **Foundational research is strongest where work develops general theories, models, and guarantees**, such as causal-inference assumptions, centrality and diffusion theory, epidemic models, graph processes, approximation bounds, and mathematical optimization. **Importance: 91**

3. **Application-driven research dominates settings with immediate operational objectives**, including court prediction, disease-risk assessment, landslide detection, fraud and phishing detection, medical QA, marketplace recommendation, and credit scoring. **Importance: 90**

4. **Research often moves from foundational methods toward applied validation through datasets, benchmarks, simulations, and experiments.** Examples include epidemic and diffusion models validated on clinical or village-adoption data, retrieval methods tested on TREC/BioASQ, and graph algorithms evaluated on real networks. **Importance: 88**

5. **A later-stage or deployment-oriented emphasis is visible in real-time and production systems**, including online A/B testing, live recommender systems, commercial marketplace optimization, stream processing, adaptive monitoring, and systems evaluated by latency, throughput, clicks, sales, or other business metrics. **Importance: 86**

6. **Foundational ideas continue to be extended rather than replaced as applications mature.** Reports describe newer systems building on earlier optimizers, geographic topic models, Apache SystemML, classical close reading, PureSVD, and traditional retrieval or ranking methods. **Importance: 82**

7. **Application pressures generate new foundational problems**, especially around fairness, bias, privacy, explainability, robustness, data quality, uncertainty, and temporal adaptation. These concerns turn practical failures and deployment constraints into new general methods and theory. **Importance: 84**

8. **Overall, the reports suggest a cyclical balance:** foundational research supplies reusable concepts and guarantees; application-driven research tests and adapts them in concrete settings; practical requirements then motivate further foundational work. **Importance: 94**

a113f03188ba9b1c5a96035e3772689e5a4903b2.text:
- **Urban and city-scale datasets**—especially data on city structure, neighborhoods, land use, urban perceptions, and planning in places such as London, Barcelona, Argentina, and Mexico—are among the most common study settings. **Importance: 95/100**
- **Mobile-phone and mobile-network data** are frequently used to study human mobility, activity patterns, floating populations, city structure, and disease-risk zones. **Importance: 94/100**
- **Online and platform-mediated urban services**—including Airbnb, Uber, taxis, ride-sharing, and Pokémon Go—are studied for demand, pedestrian traffic, mobility, supply–demand matching, and algorithmic regulation. **Importance: 90/100**
- **Urban sensing datasets involving sensory and experiential data**—geo-referenced pictures, urban sounds, music, human sounds, odors, smell color, emotions, and restorative experiences—are used to characterize city environments. **Importance: 82/100**
- **Online ranking and recommendation environments** are studied through controlled datasets and interaction data such as clicks, interleaving outcomes, and dueling or multi-dueling bandit feedback, with emphasis on fairness and evaluation. **Importance: 80/100**
- **Social, communication, and information networks** are examined using graph and propagation data to study centrality, graphlets, virality, message diffusion, item fitness, and activating emotions. **Importance: 78/100**
- **News and multilingual media datasets** are used to analyze message propagation and viral content, including emotional and VAD-based facets. **Importance: 68/100**
- **Transportation and pedestrian-mobility environments**—including taxis, ride-sharing, urban movement, and activity patterns—are repeatedly studied as real-world settings for mobility optimization and demand analysis. **Importance: 85/100**

fe2541d7883a6663d473450dfdbe9e268d254355.text:
- **Urban mobility, activity, and spatial structure** are among the most common problems: researchers use mobile-network, taxi, ride-sharing, and other behavioral data to infer movement, floating populations, neighborhood types, land use, and pedestrian demand. **Importance: 100/100**
- **Platform-mediated urban services and resource matching** are a major theme, including Airbnb, Uber, taxis, and Pokémon Go. The work addresses demand prediction, supply–demand optimization, mobility effects, and algorithmic regulation. **Importance: 91/100**
- **Ranking quality, fairness, and evaluation** are repeatedly addressed through fairness metrics, controlled data generation, optimization, click-based evaluation, interleaving, and dueling or contextual bandits. **Importance: 89/100**
- **Network structure and information diffusion** form another substantial problem area: scalable centrality and graphlet computation, message propagation, virality, item fitness, emotions, and multilingual news are studied. **Importance: 86/100**
- **Urban health and risk allocation** is an important applied problem, especially using mobility records to detect disease-risk zones and produce maps for allocating health resources. It appears narrower than the broader mobility and platform research. **Importance: 74/100**
- **Urban sensory perception and experience**—mapping soundscapes, emotions, odors, smell color, and restorative experiences—is represented through studies in London and Barcelona, but is comparatively less extensive than mobility, ranking, or network research. **Importance: 68/100**
- **Smell-centered urban analysis** appears especially underexplored: the report describes a related smell-tagging methodology, but provides much less coverage of it than of mobile-data analytics, ranking, or diffusion. **Importance: 57/100**
- **Cross-cutting links between sensory experience, platform behavior, fairness, and diffusion** remain comparatively underdeveloped in the collection; the report presents these as separate lines of work rather than a deeply integrated research problem. **Importance: 49/100**

b2819d5f21ca2ba69c1efb4b0bf7c5d4709a48b2.text:
1. **General, reliable cross-chain interoperability** — **Importance: 96/100**  
   Cross-chain transactions and communication remain open problems, and interoperability requires more than data standardization (Reports 2, 12, 46). Research gaps include handling asynchronous networks, delays, crash failures, expired timelocks, and atomicity guarantees.

2. **Fairness and bias evaluation in ranking and recommendation** — **Importance: 95/100**  
   Existing work addresses presentation bias, examination bias, popularity bias, visibility bias, and fair search, but reports also note that typical recommender metrics may not capture profitability or long-term benefits (Reports 1, 9, 17, 18, 19). A promising gap is unified evaluation that measures fairness, utility, cost, diversity, and long-term effects together.

3. **Dynamic, multilayer, and attributed community detection with interpretable evaluation** — **Importance: 93/100**  
   Community detection still faces resolution limits, threshold choice, noise, skewed degree distributions, changing graphs, overlapping communities, and heterogeneous attributes (Reports 4, 72, 73, 75). Human interpretation and characterization of detected communities remain explicit concerns (Report 74), suggesting room for methods that are scalable, statistically validated, and interpretable.

4. **Robust counterfactual and off-policy learning from biased user feedback** — **Importance: 92/100**  
   Recommendation and ranking systems rely on historical, partial, and biased feedback, while work on propensity weighting and counterfactual ranking continues to develop (Reports 1, 9, 15). Open directions include reliable evaluation under distribution shift, missing-not-at-random data, adversarial behavior, cold starts, and long-term or multi-stakeholder objectives.

5. **Approximate analytics with trustworthy, end-to-end guarantees** — **Importance: 90/100**  
   Approximate methods are used for video, graphs, joins, multidimensional data, trajectories, and cloud queries, often with error bounds or tolerances (Reports 3, 5, 8, 39, 40, 41). A research gap is combining controllable error, confidence guarantees, resource adaptation, and understandable trade-offs across complete analytical pipelines rather than isolated operators.

6. **Privacy-preserving analysis that remains useful against realistic attacks** — **Importance: 89/100**  
   Reports describe privacy-preserving cleaning, publishing, encrypted search, secure graph analysis, and privacy attacks such as text-based linkage and adversarial profiling (Reports 8, 27, 61, 66). Further work could test stronger threat models, utility under repeated or adaptive queries, and scalability across heterogeneous, dynamic, and graph-structured data.

7. **Robust learning under noisy, incomplete, and weakly labeled data** — **Importance: 87/100**  
   Many reports identify noisy or missing tuples, biased annotations, missing feedback, uncertain streams, imperfect graph attributes, and unreliable user behavior as practical obstacles (Reports 5, 6, 15, 22, 25, 51). A growing opportunity is methods that jointly model data uncertainty, annotation error, adversarial contamination, and changing distributions while providing calibrated confidence.

8. **Temporal and multimodal representation learning beyond static benchmarks** — **Importance: 85/100**  
   The reports cover dynamic relatedness, evolving graphs, sequential traces, video, multimedia recommendation, trajectories, and time-varying popularity, but many evaluations remain tied to particular datasets or domains (Reports 17, 20, 23, 25, 29, 30, 33, 34). Research could focus on representations that transfer across time, modalities, domains, and changing entity identities, with stronger evaluation under cold-start and distribution shift.
