c7ad5c91b827569ea455b3af84f619c873ca356f.text:
## Main research themes

The collection is dominated by several overlapping themes:

- **Information retrieval, search, ranking, and text mining:** including indexing, query processing, semantic retrieval, summarization, learning-to-rank, and personalization.
- **Networks and graph analytics:** including centrality, community detection, link prediction, diffusion, influence, temporal and multilayer networks, graph embeddings, and graph neural networks.
- **Databases, data management, and scalable analytics:** covering query processing, indexing, XML and relational systems, data integration, provenance, streaming, cloud systems, graph databases, and distributed processing.
- **Machine learning:** ranging from statistical models, classification, and feature engineering to deep learning, attention, reinforcement learning, adaptive methods, and graph-based learning.
- **Recommendation and personalization:** including collaborative filtering, sequential and context-aware recommendation, ranking, fairness, robustness, and multi-stakeholder systems.
- **Social media, online behaviour, and diffusion:** including misinformation, political communication, reputation, influence, virality, engagement, bots, cyberbullying, and platform safety.
- **Trust, privacy, security, data quality, and accountability:** including uncertainty, provenance, privacy-preserving analysis, fairness, explainability, auditing, and integrity.
- **Applications and specialized infrastructures:** including scholarly communication and bibliometrics, biomedical and health applications, mobility, urban sensing, finance, crowdsourcing, and scientific collaboration.

## Change from 2007 to 2020

The material does not provide year-by-year publication counts or explicit labels for 2007 and 2020, so changes in relative prominence can only be inferred qualitatively.

**Retrieval, databases, and networks remained major long-running foundations.** Earlier work was more focused on symbolic and structural problems: TF-IDF, BM25, inverted files, relational and XML queries, indexing, transactions, classical graph structure, and ranking. These themes persisted, but their scope expanded substantially.

**Networks and graph analytics became especially broad and prominent.** The emphasis moved from static structural analysis toward temporal, heterogeneous, multilayer, dynamic, predictive, and application-oriented graphs, including graph-based recommendation and scalable graph processing.

**Machine learning shifted markedly toward deep and adaptive approaches.** Conventional regression, SVMs, Bayesian models, clustering, and handcrafted features increasingly gave way to neural networks, embeddings, attention, graph neural networks, reinforcement learning, and multimodal systems.

**Social-media and diffusion research grew strongly**, changing from more abstract network and behavioural analysis toward large-scale observational and intervention-oriented studies of misinformation, influence, epidemics, engagement, and platform abuse.

**Recommendation and personalization became more central and sophisticated**, moving from collaborative filtering and similarity methods toward sequential, neural, causal, context-aware, fair, and robust systems.

Finally, **privacy, trust, fairness, and accountability became more integrated with analytics**, while **domain-specific applications diversified**. Thus, the collection appears to have shifted from primarily methodological and database-oriented research toward interconnected, scalable, socially aware, and application-driven data science.

68fcc6f2e34773701cd35d0755ae54f367bb3d9a.text:
- **Social and information networks form the largest and most diverse cluster** (importance: **95/100**). Reports cover social platforms, tagging, student and scientific collaboration networks, temporal and multilayer graphs, social-media campaigns, media-attention networks, community detection, diffusion, and influence modeling (Reports **1–3, 9–10, 12–15, 18, 24, 32–34, 38**).

- **Information retrieval is a major second cluster, spanning web, media, scientific, geographic, and conversational search** (importance: **92/100**). Core topics include topic modeling and ranking, image and visual retrieval, toponym resolution, web-quality evaluation, semantic and archival search, mobile media retrieval, biomedical extraction, and feedback-driven product search (Reports **5, 11, 16–17, 19–21, 23, 31, 39–40**).

- **Database and data-management research is comparably substantial, emphasizing scalable storage, query processing, schemas, joins, transactions, integration, uncertainty, graphs, and streaming** (importance: **90/100**). Representative areas include storage managers, XML and XPath, UCQ evaluation, distributed joins, property graphs, data fusion, privacy-preserving queries, probabilistic databases, and utility mining (Reports **4, 7, 14, 22, 26, 29, 36–38, 40–41**).

- **Digital-library work is smaller as a distinct category but distributed across scholarly documents, archives, preservation, metadata, and reproducibility** (importance: **82/100**). It includes scientific-paper summarization, citation and text-network exploration, web archives, document conversion and table extraction, digital-object preservation, scholarly platforms, bibliometric analysis, and reproducible computational assets (Reports **5, 7, 11, 18, 20, 27–29, 35**).

- **The strongest overall overlap is between information retrieval and social/information networks** (importance: **96/100**). Social data supplies retrieval signals and applications: tweet and hashtag search, user interests and behavior, social tagging, reputation and recommendation, event timelines, location-aware retrieval, engagement prediction, and conversational product feedback (Reports **1–3, 11, 13, 15, 20, 23, 31**).

- **A second very strong overlap links information retrieval with databases and data integration** (importance: **94/100**). Retrieval depends on structured storage, indexing, query processing, semantic metadata, entity resolution, knowledge bases, provenance, uncertainty handling, and integrated web, scholarly, geospatial, and multimedia data (Reports **7, 11, 20, 22, 29, 36–37, 40**).

- **The strongest digital-library overlap is with information retrieval, especially for scholarly and archival discovery** (importance: **91/100**). Summarization, citation networks, scientific-literature retrieval, historical newspaper search, archive indexing, metadata reconciliation, and biomedical knowledge discovery connect library-like collections to retrieval and ranking methods (Reports **5, 11, 18, 20, 29, 35, 39**).

- **Databases also overlap strongly with digital libraries through ingestion, preservation, provenance, and reproducibility infrastructure** (importance: **86/100**). Document conversion, structured table extraction, archive preservation, research-object management, provenance graphs, data integration, and packaged computational environments provide the underlying organization and maintenance of digital scholarly resources (Reports **7, 20, 27–29, 37**).

410481f9b0a666e61bb9596127008f7d4f10e73a.text:
1. **Graph and network science is the largest central cluster** — It includes community detection, centrality, embeddings, link prediction, graph generation, sampling, anomaly detection, diffusion, influence maximization, temporal/multilayer networks, and graph querying (Reports 5, 7, 18, 19, 21, 34, 41, 55–61, 67, 74). **Importance: 100**

2. **Scalable data systems and database/query research form a major systems cluster** — Work spans distributed databases, MapReduce, graph-processing systems, indexing, approximate and top-\(k\) querying, query optimization, data exchange, streaming, OLTP, replication, recovery, and learned database functionality (Reports 1–3, 14, 23, 27, 30, 42, 43, 56–59, 63, 75). **Importance: 96**

3. **Machine learning, recommendation, ranking, and retrieval constitute a broad application-and-method cluster** — It covers sequential and personalized recommendation, fairness-aware and counterfactual ranking, cross-modal retrieval, hashing, semantic search, bandits, explainability, and efficient representation learning (Reports 4, 25, 26, 29, 35, 40, 48, 50, 62, 64–66, 70–73). **Importance: 94**

4. **Online social-media analysis is a distinct but strongly overlapping cluster** — Sentiment, misinformation, spam, bots, cyberbullying, political behavior, social influence, cascades, trust, virality, gendered interaction, and online-community evolution are studied using Facebook, Twitter, WeChat, Reddit, Digg, WhatsApp, and other platform data (Reports 1, 4, 6, 7, 20, 22, 29, 31, 51, 52, 66, 70, 74). **Importance: 91**

5. **Data integration, knowledge representation, and data quality bridge heterogeneous information sources** — Entity resolution, schema matching, RDF/OWL exchange, ontologies, knowledge graphs, provenance, factuality, crowdsourced validation, and quality-aware retrieval connect databases, graph analytics, text mining, and biomedical or scholarly data (Reports 2, 10, 15, 27, 30, 37, 46, 49, 57, 62, 63, 71). **Importance: 89**

6. **Human–machine collaboration and crowdsourcing connect algorithmic systems to people and institutions** — Microtasks, worker motivation, aggregation, human-in-the-loop entity resolution, hybrid query systems, crowdsourced search and mapping, annotation, and collaborative knowledge construction link machine learning and databases with social and organizational research (Reports 10, 24, 36, 37, 46, 63). **Importance: 84**

7. **Scholarly communication, bibliometrics, and research infrastructure form a research-evaluation cluster** — Citation networks, research impact, preprint–publication comparison, open-access analysis, software citation, reviewer assignment, reproducibility, provenance, and EPS–HLS interdisciplinarity connect graph methods and information retrieval to science-policy and publishing questions (Reports 13, 22, 25, 33, 45, 54, 63, 71). **Importance: 82**

8. **The main bridges are shared graph representations, learning methods, and real-world data pipelines** — Graphs serve simultaneously as social networks, citation networks, knowledge graphs, mobility networks, transaction networks, and biological or medical graphs; machine learning and probabilistic models then support prediction, ranking, anomaly detection, and decision-making across them. Shared bridges also include scalable indexing/stream processing, embeddings and hashing, Bayesian or causal inference, privacy/trust mechanisms, and common datasets from social media, reviews, mobility, healthcare, and scholarly records (Reports 6, 12, 14–18, 28, 38, 41, 55, 62, 69, 72–75). **Importance: 97**

9b1cf9e02cfc986a3ddfcae8c9b118861e7f9a54.text:
1. **Graph/network analysis + machine learning and representation learning — 98/100**  
   A dominant combination involving graph embeddings, graph neural networks, community detection, node classification, link prediction, anomaly detection, and dynamic-network modeling. (Reports 4, 7, 14, 18, 21, 23, 27, 29, 41, 55, 56, 58, 60, 62, 65, 67, 74)

2. **Network analysis + information retrieval, ranking, and recommendation — 95/100**  
   Networks are repeatedly used for search, semantic retrieval, ranking, query expansion, recommendation, and personalization, including graph-based retrieval and social-search systems. (Reports 1, 4, 29, 31, 35, 48, 57, 62, 65, 66, 71, 72, 73)

3. **Databases/data management + machine learning and AI — 92/100**  
   This includes learned database systems, ML-based transaction scheduling, query generalization, large-scale ML platforms, learned indexing, entity resolution, data-quality modeling, and ML-aware query processing. (Reports 1, 3, 14, 23, 24, 30, 42, 46, 57, 63, 75)

4. **Social-media/text analytics + network structure and information diffusion — 91/100**  
   Sentiment, linguistic features, misinformation, social ties, cascades, influence, rumor detection, and diffusion are frequently studied together. (Reports 2, 4, 6, 7, 20, 28, 29, 51, 52, 55, 59, 60, 62, 70, 74)

5. **Machine learning + recommendation and personalization — 89/100**  
   Recommendation research commonly combines latent-factor models, sequence learning, graph learning, bandits, reinforcement learning, user modeling, contextual information, and ranking. (Reports 4, 22, 25, 29, 47, 62, 65, 66, 70, 72, 73)

6. **Multimodal data/computer vision + efficient retrieval and hashing — 84/100**  
   Image, video, text, and cross-modal retrieval are combined with deep features, semantic hashing, graph indexes, recommendation, and approximate nearest-neighbor search. (Reports 4, 26, 31, 40, 48, 60, 64, 72)

7. **Crowdsourcing/human computation + databases, cloud systems, and machine learning — 77/100**  
   Research combines human judgments with query processing, data integration, cloud computation, aggregation, privacy, relevance assessment, and hybrid human–machine systems. (Reports 10, 24, 30, 36, 37, 46, 63, 71)

8. **Domain-specific science or healthcare + data mining, knowledge graphs, and predictive modeling — 76/100**

a60173e78e6214441e43780ea4a1f5c38bbb6aea.text:
- **Privacy is a central design constraint when data concerns identifiable people or behavior.** It appears in mobile-phone records, social-media data, clickstreams, personal usage data, crowdfunding, and sensitive databases, motivating differential privacy, synthetic data, privacy controls, encrypted computation, and restrictions on sharing personal data (Reports 14, 34–37, 73). **Importance: 100**

- **Anonymization is treated as a trade-off rather than an absolute solution.** Systems generate synthetic clickstreams or anonymize graphs to preserve utility, while other work studies deanonymization and fraud attribution, showing that privacy protections can conflict with recommender accuracy, network analysis, or accountability (Reports 34, 36, 60). **Importance: 93**

- **Fairness becomes most visible when analytical or recommendation systems allocate opportunities, exposure, credit, or influence.** Examples include credit scoring and microlending, multi-stakeholder and online-dating recommendation, exposure allocation, group-property estimation, inclusive community detection, and influence maximization; concerns include unfair discrimination, disparate treatment, disparate impact, popularity bias, and influence disparity (Reports 14, 42, 45, 48, 50, 51, 68, 74). **Importance: 96**

- **Responsible data use is especially explicit in high-stakes applications.** Financial inclusion, epidemic surveillance, clinical retrieval, public-health modeling, crisis response, and health-related search use sensitive or consequential data and therefore foreground ethical/privacy regulations, data protection, uncertainty, and limits on interpretation or intervention (Reports 7, 14, 33, 50, 61, 72). **Importance: 95**

- **Accountability appears through provenance, explainability, auditability, and attribution.** Data provenance tracks industrial data from generation through preparation; explainable queries make log analysis more transparent; workflow provenance models hidden-data propagation; plagiarism/news provenance identifies sources; and fraud systems attribute manipulation to responsible actors (Reports 6, 11, 29, 37, 40, 60). **Importance: 91**

- **Open and collaborative data systems make governance and quality control more visible.** Open citation infrastructure emphasizes public-control services, community contributions, interoperable models, coverage gaps, and citation-data quality; collaborative dataset versioning supports branching, merging, repair, and curation (Reports 21, 23). **Importance: 84**

- **Privacy and fairness concerns intensify when data is reused across contexts or combined with inferred attributes.** Examples include nationality or ethnicity inference from contact lists, personality prediction from smartphone logs, social and demographic inference from mobility data, and identity or preference modeling in online networks (Reports 12, 14–16, 20, 70). **Importance: 90**

- **These concerns become more visible when systems influence public discourse, reputation, or collective behavior.** Social-media leakage, culturally sensitive privacy, misinformation, hate speech, political polarization, voting and blame attribution, reputation systems, search-rank fraud, and recommendation manipulation expose the need for responsible collection, interpretation, ranking, and intervention (Reports 22, 47, 51, 60, 67, 72–75). **Importance: 94**

6599b190ed38e16aef1a4d5159a53af28f34b142.text:
- **The reports do not provide a single explicit historical timeline**, so the shift between foundational and application-driven research must be inferred from the kinds of work described rather than from publication dates. **Importance: 95**

- **Foundational research is prominent in formal models, algorithms, and theory**, including Bayesian models, automata and logic, graph algorithms, PageRank, spectral methods, differential equations, causal identification, complexity analysis, and NP-hardness results (Reports 2, 5, 12, 18, 21, 23, 34, 57). **Importance: 90**

- **Application-driven research is equally substantial**, using real operational datasets and addressing concrete needs such as vaccination monitoring, maritime intelligence, dermatological diagnosis, commuter analysis, epidemic surveillance, recommendation, advertising, and healthcare (Reports 8, 9, 15, 28, 38, 39, 47, 73). **Importance: 88**

- **The balance increasingly appears to move from isolated foundational methods toward integration with real data and deployed systems**: theoretical techniques are embedded in databases, search engines, distributed platforms, workflows, and decision-support tools (Reports 3, 14, 24, 42, 63, 75). **Importance: 86**

- **Application needs often drive extensions of foundational methods**, such as dynamic graph models for evolving networks, adaptive estimation for irregular vaccination data, counterfactual ranking for presentation bias, and privacy- or fairness-aware ranking and recommendation (Reports 9, 35, 41, 66, 70, 73). **Importance: 84**

- **Evaluation becomes more empirical and application-centered in many strands**, relying on large social-media, transaction, mobility, medical, scholarly, and sensor datasets, with measures such as accuracy, latency, scalability, robustness, cost, coverage, and societal impact (Reports 1, 4, 13, 22, 31, 49, 55). **Importance: 82**

- **Foundational and applied research increasingly co-evolve rather than replace one another**: theoretical advances such as graph embeddings, probabilistic inference, optimization, and causal models are repeatedly validated through domain applications, while application constraints motivate new theory and algorithms (Reports 18, 28, 58, 62, 69, 72). **Importance: 80**

- **Overall, the reports suggest a progression toward a more balanced, translational model over time**—foundational concepts remain necessary, but research increasingly emphasizes end-to-end usefulness, adaptation to changing data, deployment constraints, trust, privacy, fairness, and reproducibility (Reports 14, 23, 25, 42, 49, 66, 75). **Importance: 92**

cebe4247ac11a5dec4d2b02bb1c7657e8961d7b7.text:
1. **Community detection became more sophisticated and inclusive (95/100).** Research progressed from modularity, spectral partitioning, and stochastic blockmodels to dynamic/topic blockmodels, multilayer graphs, hypergraph motifs, heterogeneous-network meta-paths, and methods that reduce bias against low-degree users through inclusive community detection (Reports 17, 48, 52, 57, 68).

2. **Influence analysis expanded from ranking nodes to modeling strategic influence. (94/100)** PageRank, HITS, centrality, and topic-sensitive ranking established ways to measure node importance; later work addressed influence maximization, seed selection, competing campaigns, misinformation prevention, budget constraints, fairness, and adaptive reinforcement-learning strategies (Reports 18, 19, 26, 63, 74).

3. **Diffusion research moved toward dynamic, probabilistic, and multi-context models (95/100).** Studies developed heat and opinion diffusion, SIR and percolation models, independent-cascade and linear-threshold models, temporal point processes, Hawkes processes, epidemic models, and source localization. These models were applied to rumors, innovation, popularity, disease, social media, and infrastructure disruption (Reports 17–19, 52, 57, 72–75).

4. **Graph representation increasingly relied on embeddings and learned representations (91/100).** Graph embeddings, name embeddings, query/workload embeddings, joint temporal embeddings, HIN embeddings, graph neural networks, and semantic hashing were used for link prediction, similarity, recommendation, retrieval, clustering, entity inference, and popularity prediction. Embeddings also enabled shared spaces across modalities and heterogeneous relations (Reports 16, 17, 18, 20, 36, 45, 49, 56, 57, 69).

5. **Network evolution and structure became central analytical objects. (89/100)** Research addressed link prediction, link dissolution, preferential attachment, homophily, triangle closure, community evolution, dynamic network reconstruction, signed-network balance, opinion polarization, and organizational or knowledge-network structure. These methods increasingly combined topology with attributes, behavior, and temporal observations (Reports 20, 25, 46, 47, 51, 62, 67).

6. **Graph research scaled to heterogeneous, temporal, multilayer, and higher-order networks. (88/100)** Instead of treating networks as simple one-mode graphs, studies incorporated typed relations, bipartite structures, multiplex interactions, temporal reachability, hypergraph motifs, graph streams, and higher-order cascade patterns, while developing distributed clustering, indexing, compression, and scalable PageRank methods (Reports 4, 17, 48, 52, 57, 65, 73).

7. **Applications broadened from web and citation ranking to social, scientific, commercial, health, and urban systems. (86/100)** Network methods supported scholarly influence and collaboration analysis, expert and reviewer selection, recommendation, online popularity, mobility and traffic modeling, epidemic surveillance, financial inclusion, organizational inference, political communication, and crisis or misinformation analysis (Reports 14, 15, 18, 23, 26, 50, 54, 72).

8. **Privacy became an integrated concern in graph and network analytics. (93/100)** Research developed differential-privacy mechanisms for statistical queries, social networks, clustering, spatial data, and synthetic data; it also studied graph anonymization and deanonymization, privacy-preserving clickstreams, secure embeddings, privacy-aware recommendation, encrypted search, privacy leakage, and the tension between data utility, influence analysis, and participation behavior (Reports 34–37, 48, 73).

369bb20a3df821160cbfd566a44d7674ca873600.text:
- **The corpus shows substantial reliance on widely used social-media platforms and their datasets**, especially Facebook, Twitter, Reddit, WeChat, LinkedIn, Google, and related online services. These platforms recur across sentiment analysis, cascades, political prediction, recommendation, search, advertising, and network studies, indicating concentration around a small set of major ecosystems. **Importance: 95/100** (Reports 4, 6, 7, 22, 35, 50, 61, 66, 70)

- **Several established benchmark datasets are repeatedly used for evaluation**, including Gowalla and Dianping for geo-social queries, MIMIC-III for biomedical graphs, ImageNet-derived features, Labeled Faces in the Wild, Pang Lee Polarity, the football World Cup dataset, and public recommendation datasets. This improves comparability, but can make reported progress dependent on a limited collection of familiar benchmarks. **Importance: 92/100** (Reports 1, 5, 15, 25, 26, 40)

- **Widely adopted software and cloud platforms are also prominent**, including MapReduce, Hadoop, Hive, Spark, Flink, GraphLab, OpenStack, Keras, PyData, LensKit, and MTurk/Mechanical Turk. Their use supports implementation reuse and replication, but may concentrate experiments around the capabilities, defaults, and constraints of particular platforms. **Importance: 84/100** (Reports 24, 36, 37, 42, 56, 65)

- **Reliance is significant but not universal**: the corpus also contains domain-specific or locally collected data, such as AIS vessel records, Australian census data, CDRs and GPS traces, RFID conference data, e-MID interbank data, clinical workflows, and specialized medical or mobility datasets. Thus, the corpus is benchmark-heavy in several fields, but includes substantial bespoke and application-specific evaluation. **Importance: 86/100** (Reports 3, 8, 17, 38, 41, 47, 49)

- **Platform-controlled and proprietary data create direct reproducibility risks.** Examples include Facebook advertising exposure data, LinkedIn search and salary data, eBay search data, Google localized-search results, and historical feedback or intervention logs. Repeating experiments may depend on access permissions, APIs, platform-specific collection procedures, or data that are no longer available in the same form. **Importance: 94/100** (Reports 22, 35, 50, 66, 70)

- **Temporal and platform drift threaten replication even when datasets are accessible.** The reports describe evolving social networks, streaming data, changing user behavior, concept drift, dynamic search results, and non-stationary information environments. Results obtained from historical snapshots may therefore not reproduce on later platform data. **Importance: 90/100** (Reports 6, 7, 20, 21, 42, 55, 65, 70)

- **Dataset construction and partitioning can materially change results.** The census report shows that anonymity-policy-driven partition resolutions altered commuter totals and network structure, while sampling choices affect graph-training and probe sets. This suggests that undocumented preprocessing, sampling, geographic partitioning, or resolution choices can undermine reproducibility even with the same nominal source dataset. **Importance: 91/100** (Reports 17, 38, 53, 58)

- **Benchmark comparability is weakened by inconsistent evaluation protocols and dataset robustness.** The reports explicitly note that public-dataset protocols, offline versus online evaluation, item weighting, dataset robustness, and evaluation choices affect comparisons across papers. Reproducibility therefore requires not only the dataset or platform, but also matching versions, splits, preprocessing, access conditions, and evaluation procedures. **Importance: 96/100** (Reports 25, 63, 65)

24033245cde81f688395754627d74f143acc0eb0.text:
## Topics that declined or were replaced

- **Keyword-based information retrieval** (TF-IDF, BM25, vector-space models, and relevance feedback) increasingly gave way to neural, semantic, contextual, and embedding-based ranking, including BERT and semantic hashing.
- **Unsupervised hashing** was superseded by supervised, semantic, multimodal, graph-based, and deep hashing methods.
- **Classical recommender systems**—matrix factorization, collaborative filtering, nearest neighbors, and popularity methods—were increasingly supplemented or replaced by deep, sequential, attention-based, and graph-based approaches.
- **Static, single-layer, or time-aggregated network analysis** declined relative to temporal, multilayer, multiplex, event-graph, and link-stream models.
- **Sliding-window stream models** were challenged by time-decaying influence models.
- **Naive or schema-dependent entity resolution** gave way to learned, schema-agnostic, transfer-learning, and human–machine approaches.
- **Traditional finance-based company profiling** was expanded or replaced by employee-generated reviews and salary data.
- **Shortest-distance or shortest-time navigation** was extended by pleasant-route recommendation, which incorporates beauty, quietness, and happiness.
- **Monolithic document-conversion architectures** were replaced by asynchronous microservices.
- **Archive-centric preservation** shifted toward data-centric and autonomic preservation.
- **The aging PlanetMath portal** was replaced by the Planetary System.
- **Supervised toponym resolution** was challenged by coherent unsupervised approaches, particularly for unseen place names.
- **Conventional retrieval for evolving news stories** became less adequate, encouraging adaptive representations.
- **Simple majority voting** became insufficient for noisy crowdsourcing, leading to preference models, quality models, weighted voting, phased workflows, and human–machine systems.
- **Exact set-similarity processing** was challenged by randomized, sketching, and approximate methods.
- **Traditional relational optimization** was extended by optimizers for black-box, distributed data-flow and declarative-ingestion systems.

## Topics that stabilized as baselines

- **R-tree indexing** remained an established baseline, although specialized and learned indexes such as SAR-tree and Flood improved performance.
- **Exact or conventional retrieval**, including BM25 and attribute-based search, remained baselines beside neural, semantic, graph, and approximate retrieval.
- **Exact joins** such as PPJoin, AdaptJoin, and GroupJoin remained established despite faster approximate alternatives.
- **Raw citation counts** continued to underpin impact measurement, while normalized indicators, citation networks, and altmetrics supplemented them.
- **Sliding-window models**, majority voting, and conventional network models likewise remained basic reference points despite newer alternatives.
- **Author-network self-citation** largely stabilized overall, even though author self-citation increased over time.
- **Open citation infrastructure** expanded, but the coverage gap persisted.

25af8a59514b56e730ba9f3dde2387226de4a754.text:
- **National football-team ranking from World Cup match graphs** — PageRank with restarts, custom link weighting from wins/goals, and comparison with FIFA rankings form a highly specialized, self-contained application. **Importance: 98/100** (Report 5)

- **AIS-based maritime intelligence** — Vessel trajectory prediction and anomaly detection using AIS databases, including an extreme learning machine, appear largely disconnected from the corpus’s dominant social, graph, and database applications. **Importance: 96/100** (Report 8)

- **Adaptive vaccination-uptake estimation** — Estimating uptake for 12-year-olds from web-search time series, while adapting to irregular temporal fluctuations caused by media attention or supply problems, is unusually specific. **Importance: 95/100** (Report 9)

- **Atomic cross-chain transactions in asynchronous networks** — The ac3wn protocol, permissionless witness networks, hashlocks, timelocks, and crash/delay conditions constitute a narrow blockchain-coordination niche. **Importance: 94/100** (Report 11)

- **Dermatological decision support and training** — Dermtrainer’s specialized image library, clinical diagnostic algorithm, differential-diagnosis reasoning, and disease-ranking components represent a distinctive medical application area. **Importance: 92/100** (Report 39)

- **Explanation-based auditing of electronic health-record access logs** — Template discovery and user-centered explanations for detecting misuse of sensitive medical-record access are narrowly focused compared with the broader explainability and healthcare work. **Importance: 90/100** (Report 49)

- **Census-based commuter-network resampling** — Correcting partitioning and anonymity-policy artifacts in Australian census commuting data through a surrogate high-resolution database is a particularly specific data-governance and mobility application. **Importance: 88/100** (Report 17)

- **Leaf-Removal cores and Core Influence for minimal vertex cover** — The specialized decomposition of graphs into core-breaking and maximal-matching stages, tied to P/NP complexity, appears as an isolated theoretical graph-method niche. **Importance: 86/100** (Report 34)

a8971bc5652d523d5155bcdfb4898af088cb954e.text:
1. **Research increasingly targets unstructured text and user-generated content rather than only relational records.** Sentiment analysis, opinion mining, misinformation, cyberbullying, reviews, tweets, employee comments, and conversational data are prominent applications (Reports 4, 6, 22, 29, 32, 50, 70). — **Importance: 96/100**

2. **Multimodal retrieval and representation learning have become major research themes.** Work combines images, video, text, semantic features, social context, and auxiliary modalities through cross-modal hashing, semantic video indexing, multimodal search, and image recommendation (Reports 4, 26, 40, 59, 72). — **Importance: 95/100**

3. **Streaming and continuously changing data are explicit targets of algorithms and systems.** Research addresses graph streams, topic-tree streams, IoT streams, online learning, evolving clustering, anomaly detection, behavior-change detection, and continuous query processing (Reports 2, 27, 29, 42, 44, 55, 69). — **Importance: 94/100**

4. **Traditional database and query-processing work is being extended with learned, neural, and adaptive methods.** Flood and DeepDB pursue learned DBMS functionality; neural models support query generalization, retrieval, ranking, and semantic matching; adaptive indexing and online query re-optimization address changing workloads (Reports 1, 23, 37, 42, 57, 62). — **Importance: 91/100**

5. **Graph and network data increasingly serve as the central data model for dynamic, heterogeneous information.** Research moves beyond static relational structures toward temporal, multilayer, attributed, heterogeneous, and evolving graphs, with embeddings, graph neural networks, dynamic indexes, and graph-stream summaries (Reports 18, 21, 41, 55, 56, 60, 63). — **Importance: 93/100**

6. **Large-scale social, mobility, sensor, and behavioral traces have become important experimental data sources.** Examples include Facebook and Twitter activity, mobile-phone records, GPS and check-in data, passive WiFi sensing, AIS vessel trajectories, RFID proximity, and urban sensor data (Reports 3, 6, 8, 38, 47, 53, 72, 73). — **Importance: 90/100**

7. **Querying is increasingly framed as exploratory, approximate, semantic, or interactive retrieval over noisy heterogeneous data.** Examples include approximate query processing, progressive enrichment, semantic search, question-based file retrieval, conversational search, snippets, entity resolution, and human–machine query systems (Reports 30, 31, 35, 37, 46, 59, 62, 70). — **Importance: 89/100**

8. **Machine learning has shifted from being an auxiliary database technique to a core mechanism for data management and analysis.** Deep learning, reinforcement learning, embeddings, neural ranking, learned hashing, causal prediction, and online/bandit learning are applied across retrieval, recommendation, indexing, classification, and network analysis (Reports 4, 14, 23, 24, 26, 35, 64, 73). — **Importance: 92/100**

63623e0a94c97385a54be75c3ce5ca90b6f6ac0b.text:
- **Systems-oriented contributions are highly prominent across the reports (95/100).** Many communities build or evaluate complete operational systems and infrastructure, including industrial data platforms, log-centralization systems, ingestion engines, search engines, indexing pipelines, citation infrastructures, recommender systems, and workflow platforms (Reports 6, 8, 11, 23, 24, 36, 40, 45).

- **Systems work is often tied to deployment and operational constraints rather than only abstract methods (90/100).** Reports emphasize scalability, storage, throughput, fault tolerance, privacy, energy, hardware limits, governance, and real-time performance—for example in industrial analytics, Lucene indexing, distributed ingestion, sensor networks, and cloud privacy systems (Reports 6, 8, 24, 34, 38, 41).

- **Algorithmic research is at least as pervasive as systems research and is deeply embedded within those systems (96/100).** The reports repeatedly present new algorithms and models for ranking, retrieval, graph analysis, diffusion, recommendation, clustering, query optimization, prediction, and multimodal learning (Reports 2, 4, 7, 17–20, 40, 44, 45, 57).

- **Empirical research is also extremely prominent (94/100).** Most contributions evaluate methods or systems on real, synthetic, or benchmark datasets using measures such as throughput, accuracy, MAP, click-through rate, payment success, cost, scalability, privacy loss, or user ratings (Reports 4, 5, 7, 10, 13, 18, 31, 43, 48, 52).

- **Theoretical contributions are substantial but more concentrated than systems, algorithmic, or empirical work (75/100).** Formal modeling, proofs, complexity analysis, convergence guarantees, optimization guarantees, and theoretical frameworks appear in areas such as network dynamics, query evaluation, privacy, diffusion, and hierarchical networks, but are often paired with algorithms or applications (Reports 3, 19, 34, 40, 46, 62, 65, 74).

- **User-centered research is clearly present but generally less dominant than systems and algorithmic work (78/100).** It appears through user behavior modeling, interactive search, participant evaluations, human-assisted systems, personalization, explainability, fairness, privacy, and social-platform studies (Reports 22, 31, 35, 41–43, 50, 54, 66).

- **The strongest user-centered contributions are integrated into technical systems rather than standing alone.** Human evaluation and user behavior commonly guide route recommendation, search ranking, recommender systems, crowdsourcing, online voting, and social platforms, while the core contribution remains a computational method or deployed system (Reports 22, 31, 41, 43, 54, 61, 66).

- **Overall, the corpus suggests a systems-and-algorithms-oriented community with extensive empirical validation: systems contributions are more prominent than purely theoretical or purely user-centered work, while algorithmic and empirical contributions are similarly central and frequently inseparable from the systems themselves (92/100).**

4ffcd61e62dc923ea59c766d4facd037cc17213c.text:
1. **Information retrieval, search, and ranking** — **Importance: 100/100**  
   A dominant problem family includes document retrieval, learning-to-rank, query expansion, semantic search, scholarly search, question answering, entity-set search, and multimodal retrieval. These recur across Reports 4, 7, 36, 39, 43, 49, 50, 61, 64, and 66.

2. **Network analysis, diffusion, influence, and evolution** — **Importance: 100/100**  
   Many reports study network structure, community detection, link prediction, information or epidemic diffusion, influence maximization, centrality, opinion dynamics, signed networks, and network inference. This is especially prominent in Reports 2, 17–20, 26, 46, 67, 71, and 74.

3. **Recommendation, personalization, and behavior prediction** — **Importance: 96/100**  
   Recommender systems address personalization, sequential behavior, cold starts, fairness, reciprocal and multi-stakeholder matching, popularity prediction, engagement, and robust evaluation. Reports 18, 42–45, 49, 50, 52, and 75 repeatedly address these problems.

4. **Scalable data management, query processing, and indexing** — **Importance: 95/100**  
   A major recurring concern is handling large, heterogeneous, distributed, streaming, immutable, spatial, graph, and sensor data efficiently. Problems include query optimization, cardinality estimation, ingestion, compression, indexing, storage costs, parallelism, and real-time processing (Reports 5, 6, 8, 17, 21, 24, 33, 38, 40, 48, and 57).

5. **Machine-learning classification, extraction, and multimodal analytics** — **Importance: 91/100**  
   The collection frequently addresses classification, entity and keyphrase extraction, event detection, sentiment and misinformation analysis, document and image understanding, video retrieval, and cross-modal representation learning (Reports 9, 13, 29, 43, 51, 52, 56, 63, 64, and 72).

6. **Privacy, security, fraud, provenance, and trustworthy data use** — **Importance: 86/100**  
   Recurrent problems include differential privacy, privacy-preserving recommendation and workflows, anonymization, cloud and blockchain security, plagiarism and provenance, search-rank fraud, malware, reputation, fairness, and secure data sharing (Reports 5, 29, 34–37, 47, 60, and 73).

7. **Scholarly communication, open research, and research evaluation** — **Importance: 78/100**  
   The collection contains a substantial but narrower cluster on open-access mandates, repository deposits, citation infrastructure and coverage, scholarly retrieval, citation networks, reviewer selection, research impact, collaboration, and self-citation (Reports 1, 23, 28, 50, 54, 58, and 59). Open citation coverage and interoperability remain explicit gaps in Report 23.

8. **Comparatively underexplored: specialized real-world institutional, civic, and physical-world problems** — **Importance: 82/100**  
   Relative to the dominant retrieval, recommendation, network, and data-system themes, fewer reports address problems such as organizational-chart reconstruction (Report 25), online voting and blame attribution during disasters (Report 22), congressional party reconfiguration (Report 27), pleasant urban routing (Report 31), post-event building-inspection prioritization (Report 53), smartphone-based personality prediction (Report 70), and the historical development of a database project (Report 32). These topics appear as isolated applications rather than large, recurring research clusters.

9f16b4ab83ea9f57ab2eac5a5ccfbb04386d1637.text:
## Distribution across areas

- **Social and information networks form the largest concentration** (importance about **95–100**). The corpus frequently addresses social graphs, communities, diffusion, influence, trust, mobility, recommendation, social media, collaboration, and network dynamics.

- **Information retrieval is a major, broad cluster** (about **89–95**). It spans web, mobile, multimedia, semantic, biomedical, conversational, geographic, and archival search, as well as ranking, recommendation, question answering, similarity search, indexing, and query expansion.

- **Databases and data management constitute a comparably substantial, infrastructure-oriented cluster** (about **90–94**). Key themes include scalable storage, indexing, query processing, distributed systems, graph databases, transactions, data integration, provenance, uncertainty, streaming, entity resolution, and learned database systems.

- **Digital libraries are the smallest and most specialized cluster** (about **75–82**). They focus on scholarly and archival collections, repositories, bibliometrics, citation infrastructures, metadata, preservation, scientific workflows, reproducibility, and scholarly search.

## Strongest overlaps

The **strongest broad overlap is between information retrieval and social/information networks** (about **94–98**). Social, citation, expert, and recommendation graphs provide signals for ranking, personalization, recommendation, influence analysis, misinformation detection, content discovery, and user modeling. Conversely, retrieval methods are used to search and analyse social content and behaviour.

A second major connection is between **databases and networks** (about **91–95**). Graph databases, distributed storage, indexing, relational joins, streaming systems, and scalable graph analytics support the storage, querying, and processing of social and other network data.

**Information retrieval and databases** also overlap strongly (about **92–94**) through indexing, query processing, top-\(k\) and approximate search, semantic query rewriting, entity resolution, knowledge bases, provenance, and integrated data systems.

For the digital-library material, the **strongest specific overlap is with information retrieval** (about **88–98**), especially in scholarly search, paper recommendation, citation-context retrieval, repository discovery, archive indexing, and semantic literature search. Digital libraries also connect to networks through citation and co-authorship graphs, and to databases through metadata, provenance, preservation, ingestion, and workflow infrastructure.

The clearest **four-way convergence** is scholarly and semantic information infrastructure: libraries supply the content, retrieval enables discovery, networks provide citation and collaboration structure, and databases provide storage, indexing, provenance, and querying.

c3639b212482e1fd307e0d2efca1b81ae25b80dc.text:
- **Supervised prediction and classification remain a major foundation** (importance: **95/100**). The corpus includes deception and sockpuppetry classifiers, crisis classification, supervised toponym resolution, table-structure relation prediction using labeled data, web-quality classification, tweet-engagement prediction, and antimicrobial-consumption prediction with Elastic Net and Gaussian Processes (Reports 1, 3, 7, 13, 16, 19, 21).

- **Unsupervised and probabilistic modeling is used to discover latent structure without extensive labels** (importance: **92/100**). Examples include LDA and dynamic topic models for topics and user interests, probabilistic text-and-link models in TopicAtlas, the gazetteer-only coherent model for toponym resolution, and stochastic Yule–Simon/Poisson models for vocabulary growth (Reports 2, 11, 16, 18).

- **Unsupervised methods can approach or exceed supervised systems in data-sparse settings** (importance: **88/100**). The coherent unsupervised toponym-resolution model performs close to the state-of-the-art supervised method, does better when toponyms are unseen, and outperforms another unsupervised method and several commercial systems (Report 16).

- **Weak supervision appears explicitly where manually labeled data are limited** (importance: **90/100**). Scientific-paper summarization uses pseudo-labeled training data and a weakly supervised attention-based architecture that jointly learns cue phrases, context embeddings, and word-level attention through an LSTM encoder (Report 5).

- **Representation learning increasingly replaces or augments hand-engineered features** (importance: **94/100**). The corpus describes continuous word representations, spatial embeddings, context embeddings, attention-based encoders and decoders, language-guided visual attention, learned discrete hashing spaces, and adaptive visual representations for retrieval and evolving news (Reports 1, 3, 5, 11, 17).

- **Deep neural and graph-based representations extend learning to structured and relational data** (importance: **93/100**). Multi-graph convolution models represent symptom–symptom, symptom–herb, and herb–herb relations; recurrent variational graph convolutions learn temporal vertex representations; and GC-LSTM, graph convolution, multilayer embeddings, and graphons support temporal prediction, link prediction, recommendation, and network analysis (Reports 6, 9, 10, 34).

- **Learning becomes increasingly adaptive, online, and feedback-driven** (importance: **86/100**). Online learning personalizes mobile media retrieval, adaptive representations track evolving news stories, and pairwise deep reinforcement learning incorporates positive and negative feedback for recommendation; conversational search further decomposes negative feedback into aspect–value pairs (Reports 5, 23, 31).

- **The overall pattern is hybridization: learned models are combined with domain structure, metadata, and symbolic resources** (importance: **89/100**). Examples include gazetteers and geographic scope in unsupervised toponym resolution, knowledge bases and ontology enrichment in information extraction, graph relationships in TCM recommendation, and engineered plus learned visual features in webpage-quality ranking (Reports 16, 20, 6, 17).

af0904506bea7cc60afffa2fe2e73ba7229fdef3.text:
1. **Misinformation research has moved from simple content classification toward modeling propagation, credibility, and intervention.** Studies now analyze cascade structure and growth, rumor source detection, credibility-aware inference, misinformation containment, and cascade blocking across WeChat, Twitter, Reddit, Digg, and other platforms. *(Reports 7, 28, 62)* — **Importance: 98**

2. **Polarization is increasingly studied as a network and behavioral process rather than only as a difference in opinions.** Research examines antagonistic voter groups, political profiling, conspiracy-content consumption, celebrity-related polarization, collective emotion, controversy, and how interaction structures and diffusion shape political communities. *(Reports 6, 30, 70, 74)* — **Importance: 94**

3. **Online behavior research has become more dynamic, multimodal, and predictive.** Scholarship combines text, images, temporal activity, social graphs, mobility, interactions, and user profiles to study sentiment, virality, tie strength, community evolution, trolling, flaming, job-related moods, recommendation behavior, and behavior change. *(Reports 6, 20, 29, 31, 51, 55)* — **Importance: 92**

4. **Marketing scholarship has shifted from broad targeting toward large-scale, socially informed, and increasingly causal personalization.** Research analyzes millions of Facebook ads, measures exposure and overprofiling, models social exposure, predicts click-through rates, optimizes advertiser budgets, and uses reinforcement learning or bandits for ad placement, ranking, and recommendation. *(Reports 6, 22, 53, 67, 73)* — **Importance: 91**

5. **Safety research has broadened from detecting abuse to proactive prevention and risk reduction.** Work covers cyberbullying, cyberaggression, spam, defamation, illegitimate promotion, malicious applications, suspicious links, bots, catfish, flaming, hate speech, and privacy threats, while incorporating proactive abuse prevention and bias-aware criteria such as equalized odds. *(Reports 6, 7, 29, 51, 52)* — **Importance: 97**

6. **Trust and misinformation studies increasingly account for source quality, coordinated manipulation, and adversarial behavior.** Examples include fake reviews and elite Sybil attacks, opinion spam, source-level factuality and media-bias prediction, credibility reliability training, bot detection, and trust computation in social graphs. *(Reports 1, 7, 28, 30, 55, 66)* — **Importance: 90**

7. **Platform scholarship has become more concerned with fairness, transparency, and accountability in ranking and recommendation.** Research addresses fairness-aware ranking, demographic parity, equality of opportunity, News Feed visibility bias, fair summarization, explainable models, dataset documentation, and the interpretability of automated decisions. *(Reports 25, 48, 66, 71, 73)* — **Importance: 93**

8. **The field increasingly combines computational scale with intervention-oriented system design.** Large platform datasets and scalable graph or streaming methods support not just description, but prediction, personalized recommendation, influence maximization, rumor control, safety enforcement, and real-time monitoring—while also raising privacy and re-identification concerns. *(Reports 7, 14, 29, 42, 55, 65, 72)* — **Importance: 95**

b0ebbf7c3d705bc66bbdf0e8bb66d5390677fa4c.text:
- **Social media, online communities, and social networks** — **100/100**  
  Recur extensively in studies of diffusion, influence, opinion, misinformation, political communication, social interaction, privacy, mobility, and network structure (Reports 2, 12–20, 22, 25–27, 34–35, 44, 50–52, 58, 63–64, 67, 71–75).

- **Recommendation and personalization** — **96/100**  
  Applications include e-commerce, news, music, scholarly information, travel, online dating, products, teammates, routes, tags, videos, and social content (Reports 7, 12, 17–18, 26, 35–36, 40, 42–45, 49–52, 57, 63, 67, 75).

- **Search, information retrieval, and ranking** — **94/100**  
  Repeated across web search, query understanding, semantic search, document retrieval, ranking, digital libraries, image/video retrieval, patent search, and specialized search systems (Reports 4, 7–9, 26, 36, 39–40, 43, 48–50, 59–61, 64–66, 69).

- **Data management, databases, and large-scale analytics** — **92/100**  
  Recurring applications involve database systems, indexing, data ingestion, data integration, query optimization, provenance, stream and sensor data, repositories, versioning, and scalable analytics (Reports 5–6, 11, 17, 21, 24, 33–34, 37–40, 48, 52, 56–58, 63, 65).

- **Scholarly communication and research infrastructure** — **88/100**  
  Includes open access, repositories, citation networks, scholarly search, publication recommendation, reviewer selection, research impact, scientific collaboration, and open citation data (Reports 1–2, 7, 23, 28, 30, 39, 49–51, 54, 58–61, 65).

- **Security, privacy, fraud, and trust** — **84/100**  
  Applications include blockchain integrity, privacy-preserving recommendation and data management, plagiarism, malware and search-rank fraud, reputation systems, cloud security, secure workflows, and misinformation protection (Reports 5, 18, 22, 29, 34–37, 47, 60, 73–75).

- **Mobility, transportation, and urban applications** — **76/100**  
  Recur in human-mobility modeling, commuting, mall visitation, traffic optimization, ride-sharing, pleasant-route recommendation, epidemic mobility, and mobility-based social analysis (Reports 2, 14–15, 19, 26, 31, 43, 53, 55, 67, 71).

- **Health, epidemiology, and biomedical applications** — **70/100**  
  Appear in clinical information retrieval, epidemic surveillance and modeling, disease containment, biomedical publication retrieval, drug-recall prediction, health search, public-health sensing, and medical imaging (Reports 7, 14, 33, 39, 43, 50, 59, 61, 63–64, 66, 72).

96f31c06ee06146c39f43065947e16c2143e1e0d.text:
1. **Privacy is a focused methodological concern rather than a pervasive theme.** It is most explicit in privacy-preserving profile matching over decentralized mobile social networks, secure transmission, secret answers, personal-knowledge extraction, privacy-preserving data publishing, and privacy-preserving transformations of uncertain data. **Importance: 95**

2. **Privacy and disclosure concerns become more visible when data are personal, distributed, or publicly exposed.** Examples include mobile social-network profiles, social-media and location data, personalized retrieval, web archives, and open-government-data reuse, where the reports note disclosure, access, latency, or capacity concerns. **Importance: 91**

3. **Anonymization is not a prominent standalone concept in the reports.** The corpus emphasizes privacy-preserving computation, secure channels, data publishing, and uncertainty resulting from privacy transforms more than explicit anonymization or de-identification techniques. **Importance: 84**

4. **Fairness appears mainly through unequal access, representation, and measurement.** Location-based accessibility work studies spatial inequality and exclusion; the engineering campaign addresses gender diversity; and bibliometric work seeks unbiased national comparisons under changing publication distributions. **Importance: 88**

5. **Fairness and bias become especially visible when rankings, recommendations, or evaluations affect people or institutions.** Examples include reputation and review systems, university rankings, personalized retrieval, recommendation, web-quality assessment, and national research-performance indicators, where weights, engagement, data distributions, or attribution can advantage some groups or entities. **Importance: 82**

6. **Accountability is represented through provenance, reproducibility, governance, and traceability.** Fine-grained table-cell provenance, provenance graphs, retrospective provenance queries, computational-asset packaging, virtualization, reproducibility publications, and self-governing-community analysis all support checking how data and results were produced or governed. **Importance: 94**

7. **Responsible data use is also expressed through data quality, truth discovery, uncertainty handling, and source accountability.** The reports describe conflict identification, source-accuracy estimation, source correlation, multiple truths, uncertainty-aware databases, repair mechanisms, expert reliability based on review histories, and evidence-based project selection. **Importance: 90**

8. **These concerns become most visible in large-scale, sensitive, or consequential applications.** They surface around health and biomedical data, mobility and social networks, public archives and government data, research evaluation and funding, automated recommendations, and systems used for surveillance or decision support; they are less visible in infrastructure, storage, compression, and purely algorithmic-performance studies. **Importance: 89**

109a28b9a3102d2e94311f4c1f365d1be8d22f8a.text:
1. **The corpus shows substantial reliance on established benchmark datasets and standard collections.** Information retrieval work explicitly evaluates on TREC and other standard collections; recommendation research uses MovieLens, Amazon Movies, Epinions, Ciao, and session-based datasets; classification uses Reuters-21578, TDT2, UK 2006/2007, Wiki, and multilingual corpora. **Importance: 96**

2. **A relatively small set of platforms recurs across many communities.** Twitter, Reddit, Flickr, Wikipedia, Amazon, Booking.com, YouTube, Google, Bing, Yahoo, Lucene, PostgreSQL, Jupyter, Spark, and Semantic Scholar appear as data sources, evaluation environments, or deployment platforms. **Importance: 94**

3. **Social-media platforms are especially concentrated sources of empirical data.** Twitter and Reddit support repeated work on diffusion, misinformation, voting, popularity, politics, search, and network analysis, while Flickr, Instagram, Facebook, and mobile-platform data support related behavioral and multimedia studies. **Importance: 91**

4. **The corpus also relies on domain-specific flagship datasets and shared-task resources.** Examples include MNIST and Caltech101 for vision, the Million Song Dataset and 300 Jazz Standards for music, Spider for query synthesis, Wiki-Flickr Event for multimodal retrieval, CrisisMMD for disaster analysis, and MediQA 2019 for medical NLP. **Importance: 82**

5. **This concentration suggests benchmark and platform bias: findings may reflect the properties of frequently reused datasets rather than broad real-world conditions.** The reports repeatedly evaluate methods on particular social, scholarly, commercial, or multimedia collections, which can privilege specific user populations, domains, languages, interaction patterns, and network structures. **Importance: 87**

6. **Dependence on commercial platforms and restricted behavioral data creates reproducibility risks.** Reports describe transaction logs, clickstreams, personal usage data, search logs, and platform data whose availability is limited by privacy policies or platform access; Booking.com, Walmart, Taobao, Google, Bing, Yahoo, and other systems are prominent examples. **Importance: 92**

7. **Dataset coverage and incompleteness are explicit concerns even for open scholarly infrastructure.** OpenCitations reports a persistent citation-coverage gap, while other work depends on changing repositories, social-platform streams, and archived or versioned data. These conditions can make exact replication difficult as coverage, APIs, platform behavior, or dataset versions change. **Importance: 89**

8. **Reproducibility is partly supported by open and reusable infrastructure, but unevenly.** Open datasets and repositories such as COCI, OpenCitations, arXiv, DBLP, CiteSeerX, public benchmark collections, open-source systems, DataHub, and Git-inspired version control improve access and traceability; however, the corpus simultaneously includes proprietary, privacy-constrained, synthetic, and platform-dependent data, producing uneven replication prospects. **Importance: 90**

592a9895c4c7297ec20aedca8be9f874ae29f557.text:
1. **Network analysis + information retrieval, ranking, and recommendation — 98/100**  
   Combines graph structure, centrality, embeddings, citation or social networks, search, ranking, and recommender systems. Appears across expert finding, PageRank, scholarly discovery, social recommendation, graph search, and semantic retrieval (Reports 7, 26, 43, 44, 49, 50, 54, 61, 64, 67, 73).

2. **Databases/data management + machine learning and analytics — 96/100**  
   Integrates relational databases, query processing, indexing, data integration, distributed systems, and learned models such as regression, embeddings, cost models, and predictive queries (Reports 5, 6, 17, 21, 24, 33, 40, 48, 57, 63).

3. **Network analysis + machine learning, diffusion, and social behavior — 95/100**  
   Combines graph models with neural methods, link prediction, influence maximization, epidemic or information diffusion, opinion dynamics, and behavioral inference (Reports 2, 14, 17–20, 25, 46, 50, 67, 71, 72, 74).

4. **Multimodal machine learning + retrieval and classification — 91/100**  
   Brings together text, images, video, audio, speech, embeddings, neural models, and search or event retrieval. Examples include multimodal event detection, cross-modal video retrieval, music similarity, image retrieval, and multimedia monitoring (Reports 9, 12, 13, 43, 49, 52, 56, 72, 75).

5. **Social-media analysis + NLP, machine learning, and network science — 90/100**  
   Uses posts, hashtags, interaction graphs, and user behavior for sentiment, rumor, misinformation, political, health, influence, and event analysis, often combining classifiers or neural models with graph and diffusion methods (Reports 18, 19, 22, 51, 64, 67, 72, 73, 75).

6. **Scholarly communication + citation networks, information retrieval, and open-data infrastructure — 87/100**  
   Combines publication search and ranking with citation analysis, co-authorship networks, metadata matching, open citation datasets, reviewer selection, and research-impact measurement (Reports 23, 50, 54, 58, 59, 61).

7. **Privacy/security + databases, machine learning, and network analysis — 83/100**  
   Integrates differential privacy, secure data management, anonymization, encrypted search, privacy-preserving recommendation, clickstream generation, and graph analysis (Reports 29, 34–37, 48, 73).

8. **Mobile/mobility data + network analysis, epidemiology, and urban analytics — 81/100**  
   Combines call-detail records, mobility traces, social-network construction, behavioral prediction, epidemic modeling, traffic analysis, and city-scale optimization (Reports 2, 14, 15, 33, 55, 72).

cfaaa4e23317a03b1afb1d581616c45decd361f0.text:
1. **From static graph analysis to temporal and dynamic networks** — Research expanded from conventional social and citation graphs to timestamped links, event graphs, link streams, multilayer adjacency matrices, and temporal neighborhoods. Models such as TNA and GC-LSTM predict future graph states, added or removed links, and newly formed temporal edges. **Importance: 98/100** (Reports 9, 10)

2. **Community detection became more structurally and computationally sophisticated** — Work progressed from social community analysis to cohesive-subgraph models such as k-VCC, which reduce the free-rider effect and enumerate overlapping communities using neighbor- and group-sweep optimizations. Multilayer research further added clique percolation, graphlets, layer similarity, and group detection across heterogeneous networks. **Importance: 95/100** (Reports 33, 34)

3. **Influence analysis moved from identifying influential users to modeling influence flows and changing influence over time** — GhostLink inferred latent influence networks and influential users; flow-based visual summarization represented influence patterns in large citation graphs; centrality measures supported seed selection and immunization; and time-decaying influence models enabled streaming analysis of social influence. **Importance: 94/100** (Reports 1, 18, 34, 38)

4. **Diffusion research broadened across social, epidemic, technological, and information settings** — Networks were used to study word-of-mouth, knowledge propagation among students, campaign momentum, epidemic and malware spread, cascading failures, and future discussion activity. Temporal and multilayer models showed that changing topology and multiple spreading routes can alter conclusions drawn from static networks. **Importance: 96/100** (Reports 1, 3, 10, 24, 34)

5. **Graph embeddings and learned representations became central to prediction and recommendation** — Spatial embeddings supported location-aware recommendation; continuous word representations supported social-media analysis; variational graph convolutions generated temporal vertex representations; and multiplex or hyperbolic embeddings represented heterogeneous multilayer relations. Graph models also supported syndrome-aware herb recommendation through symptom–symptom, symptom–herb, and herb–herb graphs. **Importance: 91/100** (Reports 3, 6, 9, 11, 34)

6. **Graph research increasingly integrated heterogeneous, multilayer, and property-graph data** — Research moved beyond single edge types toward multiplex networks, interdependent cyber-physical systems, provenance graphs, property graphs, graph schemas, and synthetic graph benchmarks. These developments supported network fusion, provenance queries, scalability testing, and analysis of graph structure and attacker strength. **Importance: 89/100** (Reports 29, 34, 37)

7. **Privacy became part of graph mining and network data management rather than a separate concern** — Privacy-preserving profile matching was implemented for decentralized, multi-hop mobile social networks, while privacy also appeared in data publishing, secure transmission, secret answers, personal knowledge extraction, and privacy-preserving transformations. Work on disclosure concerns, source contributions, and attacker-controlled synthetic graphs further connected privacy with utility and security. **Importance: 93/100** (Reports 20, 29, 36, 37, 40)

8. **Graph methods increasingly combined prediction, visualization, and scalable computation** — Research paired graph representations with recurrent models, graph convolutions, Hawkes processes, stochastic block models, graphons, flow-based visualization, distributed sketches, and efficient query or storage systems. This reflects a shift from describing network structure toward forecasting, intervention, monitoring, and interactive exploration at large scale. **Importance: 90/100** (Reports 10, 11, 18, 22, 34, 38)

b18976dbd7978e5634d13b948dd0ce16ec1010eb.text:
1. **Postgres project history and development-team organization** — **98/100**  
   Report 32 focuses narrowly on the historical leadership, student programmers, and codebase of the Postgres project, unlike the corpus’s broader database-method themes.

2. **Planetary System and social-semantic portals for mathematical/STEM documents** — **97/100**  
   Report 30’s PlanetMath replacement, eMath3.0 portals, and semantic-help/e-learning systems form a distinctive application cluster with little overlap elsewhere.

3. **Brazilian congressional party configuration and fragmentation reduction** — **96/100**  
   Report 27’s *arrange* method, roll-call-based ideology inference, party-discipline constraints, and Brazilian Congress application are unusually specific politically oriented topics.

4. **Resilience-based post-event building-inspection prioritization** — **95/100**  
   Report 53 uniquely combines seismic fragility functions, predicted building damage, expected loss, access restrictions, and integer optimization for recovery planning.

5. **Relative-state flipping in signed random dynamical networks** — **94/100**  
   Report 46 presents a highly specialized theoretical model involving signed links, stochastic Bernoulli attention, almost-sure convergence/divergence, and weakly balanced graphs.

6. **Hourglass effects in hierarchical dependency networks** — **92/100**  
   Report 3’s narrow “waist” of reusable intermediate modules, source-to-target path coverage, and dependency-network core are distinctive concepts not substantially developed in other reports.

7. **Realtime crowdsourcing through retainer worker pools** — **90/100**  
   Report 41 uniquely centers on precruitment, push notifications, queueing theory, sub-second response thresholds, and requester-cost minimization.

8. **Organizational-chart inference from enterprise social networks** — **88/100**  
   Report 25’s staged *Create* method—social stratification, supervision-link inference, and consecutive-class matching—targets a specialized enterprise-organization reconstruction problem.

29835ce193445b3eecc8323bc72361a10a294762.text:
1. **Social-media and online-community platforms** — Twitter/X, Reddit, Instagram, blogs, Facebook, Quora, and related social networks are among the most common sources for studying diffusion, sentiment, misinformation, voting, popularity, identity, and behavior. *(Reports 2, 13, 16, 18–19, 22, 44, 51, 64, 67, 72–75)* — **100/100**

2. **Scholarly publishing, citation, and research-network datasets** — Articles, citations, co-authorship, repositories, arXiv/DBLP/CiteSeerX, OpenCitations, ScienceDirect, and institutional repositories are frequently used for retrieval, impact analysis, reviewer selection, open access, and knowledge diffusion. *(Reports 1, 7, 23, 39, 49–50, 54, 58–59, 61)* — **96/100**

3. **Search engines, information-retrieval collections, and digital libraries** — Search logs, clickstreams, query datasets, web pages, digital libraries, and benchmark collections such as TREC, Reuters-21578, and Semantic Scholar are repeatedly studied for ranking, query expansion, retrieval, and search behavior. *(Reports 4, 7–8, 26, 36, 39–40, 49–50, 59–61, 64–65)* — **95/100**

4. **Recommendation, e-commerce, marketplaces, and online-service platforms** — Booking.com, Walmart, Taobao, Amazon, online dating, crowdfunding, app markets, music services, and other recommender environments provide interaction logs, ratings, purchases, reviews, and user–item behavior. *(Reports 18, 35–36, 39, 42–45, 49–50, 60, 75)* — **93/100**

5. **Mobile-phone, human-mobility, and urban-transportation data** — Call-detail records, smartphone logs, check-ins, mall visits, taxi trips, traffic networks, and mobility datasets from Santiago, New York, Berlin, Dakar, Ivory Coast, Portugal, and other cities support studies of movement, social ties, epidemics, finance, and traffic. *(Reports 2, 14–15, 19, 26, 55, 70–71)* — **91/100**

6. **Real, synthetic, and dynamic graph/network datasets** — Social, information, citation, technological, biological, face-to-face, multiplex, signed, hypergraph, and cascade networks are widely used, often alongside synthetic graphs and simulations, for diffusion, clustering, ranking, link prediction, structure, and network evolution. *(Reports 2–4, 10, 17–21, 46–48, 52, 57, 67–68, 74)* — **90/100**

7. **Multimedia, news, and multimodal datasets** — Broadcast TV/radio, images, video, audio, Flickr, YouTube, Million Song Dataset, 300 Jazz Standards, Wiki-Flickr Event, CrisisMMD, and flood imagery appear in retrieval, event detection, summarization, popularity, and cross-modal analysis. *(Reports 9, 12–13, 18, 31, 43, 49, 52, 56, 72, 75)* — **84/100**

8. **Industrial, sensor, IoT, and physical infrastructure environments** — Industrial repositories, smart factories, machine fleets, wireless sensor networks, environmental monitoring, energy systems, buildings, and traffic infrastructure are studied for real-time analytics, maintenance, optimization, resilience, and decision support. *(Reports 6, 33, 38, 53, 55, 63)* — **77/100**

7afd3869978575a862303643f61d202542dc9fe9.text:
1. **Research often progresses from foundational methods to application-driven systems.** In information retrieval, early foundations such as TF-IDF, BM25, vector-space models, and language models are followed by neural ranking, click adaptation, clinical retrieval, patent search, and recommendation applications. **Importance: 95**

2. **Foundational techniques remain active as applications expand rather than being replaced.** PageRank began as a core ranking model and was later extended through weighted, evolving, and context-sensitive variants for web pages, citations, patents, social networks, mobility, and cyber-attack prediction. **Importance: 91**

3. **Over time, research becomes increasingly oriented toward real-time and operational use.** Industrial big-data work emphasizes real-time decision making, predictive maintenance, energy management, smart factories, and supply chains, while sensor-network research optimizes energy, storage, and query costs. **Importance: 88**

4. **Application demands also stimulate new foundational work.** Mobility, electricity, social interaction, and scientific-diffusion applications motivate new models of heterogeneous networks, human behavior, uncertainty, diffusion, and network formation. **Importance: 86**

5. **Established research projects can begin with foundational system-building before broader application and recognition.** The Postgres project, developed mainly in the mid-1980s to mid-1990s, centered on database design ideas and codebase development, illustrating an earlier emphasis on core infrastructure. **Importance: 76**

6. **Later research increasingly combines foundational theory with domain-specific deployment and evaluation.** Semantic data mining links formal frameworks such as CRISP-DM, process reuse, and semantic analysis to business intelligence, decision support, epidemic modeling, recommendation, cancer diagnosis, and education. **Importance: 83**

7. **The balance is not a simple one-way shift: foundational and applied work continue in parallel.** Reports describe theoretical models—such as diffusion processes, signed-network dynamics, query optimization, and probabilistic databases—alongside direct applications in politics, health, commerce, infrastructure, and social platforms. **Importance: 90**

8. **The reports do not provide a single longitudinal measure of the overall balance between foundational and application-driven research.** Their evidence supports a broad pattern of foundational methods being progressively extended and embedded in applications, but not a quantified historical trend across all fields. **Importance: 94**

c8165a32ecb20ee77b7bd7f13688706f25b92099.text:
1. **Complex networks, diffusion, and social dynamics — 98/100**  
   A major cluster studies network structure, centrality, link prediction, community formation, opinion dynamics, signed networks, influence maximization, cascades, and epidemic or rumor spreading (Reports 17–20, 46, 67, 71, 74). **Bridges** include shared diffusion models connecting online social networks to mobility, public health, misinformation, recommendation, and infrastructure disruption.

2. **Information retrieval, search, ranking, and recommendation — 97/100**  
   This cluster covers traditional and neural retrieval, query expansion, learning-to-rank, semantic search, scholarly search, question answering, personalization, session behavior, and recommender systems (Reports 7, 36, 39, 43, 45, 49, 50, 61). **Bridges** are embeddings, user-click and transaction data, graph-based ranking, multimodal representations, and shared evaluation practices that connect search, recommendation, social platforms, and digital libraries.

3. **Data management, scalable analytics, and query processing — 96/100**  
   A systems-oriented cluster addresses databases, indexing, compression, distributed ingestion, stream and sensor processing, query optimization, workload management, data versioning, and large-scale industrial analytics (Reports 5, 6, 8, 11, 17, 21, 24, 33, 34, 38, 40, 48, 57). **Bridges** include reusable index structures, graph and relational representations, hardware-aware optimization, provenance, and scalable infrastructure shared by industrial, scientific, privacy, and social-data applications.

4. **Semantic data, knowledge graphs, and scholarly information infrastructure — 94/100**  
   This cluster centers on RDF, SPARQL, ontologies, semantic search, entity and formula retrieval, linked data, citation networks, scholarly repositories, and research-discovery tools (Reports 23, 30, 50, 54, 58, 64, 65). **Bridges** connect formal knowledge representation with information retrieval, citation analysis, open scholarship, reviewer selection, biomedical data, educational systems, and social-semantic portals.

5. **Multimodal media, event, and content analytics — 91/100**  
   Research combines text, images, video, speech, audio, and structured data for event detection, summarization, broadcast monitoring, visual retrieval, video-moment search, popularity prediction, and multimodal classification (Reports 9, 12, 13, 43, 49, 52, 56, 72). **Bridges** are shared representation-learning and cross-modal alignment methods linking multimedia analysis to search, social-media monitoring, crisis response, recommendation, and graph-based event modeling.

6. **Human behavior, mobility, and computational social sensing — 90/100**  
   A cluster uses mobile-phone, social-media, smartphone, online-community, and location data to study movement, shopping, personality, friendship, voting, engagement, and collective behavior (Reports 2, 14–16, 22, 25, 35, 70, 72, 75). **Bridges** connect behavioral data to network science, urban traffic optimization, financial inclusion, epidemic modeling, online-platform studies, and social influence.

7. **Privacy, security, trust, and provenance — 89/100**  
   This cluster addresses differential privacy, privacy-preserving clickstreams and workflows, cloud and database security, plagiarism and provenance, reputation, fraud attribution, anonymization, and privacy-sensitive participation (Reports 29, 34–37, 47, 60, 73). **Bridges** arise because privacy and trust constraints are applied across otherwise separate areas: recommendation and search, social-network analysis, data management, workflow systems, marketplaces, and open-data infrastructures.

e22c4598ee2d50d36eaa79251aa3bd3b5319b493.text:
Across the corpus, machine learning evolves from mainly **classical supervised prediction** toward flexible, hybrid systems that combine labels, latent structure, learned representations, and feedback.

**Supervised learning remains the foundation.** Early and conventional applications use SVMs, Naive Bayes, logistic regression, k-nearest neighbors, random forests, linear models, and neural classifiers for tasks such as spam, sentiment, rumor, bot, deception, event, crisis, and web-quality detection. Supervised methods also support ranking, recommendation, diagnosis, demographic inference, entity resolution, and behavioral prediction. Over time, supervision becomes more specialized and structurally informed: models incorporate causal feature selection, social and graph features, temporal dynamics, multimodal inputs, domain adaptation, multitask learning, click and transaction logs, and counterfactual or intervention-derived information.
